 16912  
 16913      F-1 applicants will generally need to timely file their EOS 
 16914  application--meaning that USCIS will need to receive the application on 
 16915  or before the date the authorized admission period expires. See new 8 
 16916  CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B). This application timeframe for timely filing 
 16917  an EOS application will include the 30-day period of preparation for 
 16918  departure allowed after the completion of studies or any authorized 
 16919  practical training. However, if the extension application is received 
 16920  during the 30-day period of preparation for departure provided in 8 CFR 
 16921  214.2(f)(5)(v) following the completion of studies, the alien in F-1 
 16922  status may continue studying but may not continue or begin engaging in 
 16923  practical training or other employment until the extension request is 
 16924  approved and, as applicable, an EAD is issued. See new 8 CFR 
 16925  214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B). To avoid this scenario, DHS continues to encourage 
 16926  nonimmigrants to file their EOS applications within the six months 
 16927  \338\ preceding the expiration of their stay.
 16928  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16929  
 16930      \338\ With respect to the earliest filing date for a Form I-539, 
 16931  there is no prohibition on filing the form before a certain date 
 16932  ahead of expiration.
 16933  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16934  
 16935      The length of the extension granted could be up to the period of 
 16936  time needed to complete the program or requested practical training, 
 16937  not to exceed 4 years, unless the alien is a border commuter, enrolled 
 16938  in language training, or attending a public high school. By permitting 
 16939  admission only ``up to'' the prescribed period, USCIS and CBP are 
 16940  afforded discretion as to the ultimate length of time to grant the 
 16941  applicant and consider factors such as program length.
 16942      F-2 dependents seeking to accompany the F-1 principal student will 
 16943  need to file applications for an EOS or reinstatement, as applicable. 
 16944  See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iv). A dependent F-2 spouse and unmarried 
 16945  children under the age of 21 seeking to accompany the principal F-1 
 16946  student during the additional period of admission will need to either 
 16947  be included on the primary applicant's request for extension or 
 16948  properly file their own EOS applications on the form designated by 
 16949  USCIS. If the dependent files a separate Form I-539, he or she will 
 16950  need to pay a separate Form I-539 filing fee. However, if the dependent 
 16951  files a Form I-539A as part of the primary applicant's EOS request on a 
 16952  Form I-539, only one fee will be required.
 16953      USCIS generally will need to receive the extension applications on 
 16954  or before the expiration of the previously authorized period of 
 16955  admission, including the 30-day period following the completion of the 
 16956  course of study, as indicated on the F-2 dependent's I-94. To qualify 
 16957  for an EOS, the F-2 dependent will need to demonstrate the qualifying 
 16958  relationship with the principal F-1 student who is maintaining status, 
 16959  also be maintaining his or her own status, and not have engaged in any 
 16960  unauthorized employment. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iv). Extensions of 
 16961  stay for F-2 dependents will not be able to exceed the authorized 
 16962  admission period of the principal F-1 student. By removing D/S for 
 16963  family members, DHS is ensuring that a spouse who engaged in 
 16964  unauthorized employment would be denied EOSs and must return home. As 
 16965  with other nonimmigrant classifications, if a dependent is aging out 
 16966  before the program end date listed on the I-20, the entire family, 
 16967  including the J-1 principal, will receive an EOS only until the F-2's 
 16968  21st birthday, which will then require the remaining family members and 
 16969  the principal F-1 student to apply for an EOS for the remainder of the 
 16970  program and for the aged out F-2 to leave the country or change status 
 16971  to a different nonimmigrant category.

 16976  nonimmigrant classifications, they will not be given any period of time 
 16977  to prepare for departure from the United States after the denial, and 
 16978  there may be significant immigration consequences for failing to depart 
 16979  the country immediately. For example, such aliens generally will begin 
 16980  to accrue unlawful presence the day after the issuance of the denial. 
 16981  DHS
 16982  
 16983  [[Page 45111]]
 16984  
 16985  believes this standard provides parity across nonimmigrant 
 16986  classifications.
 16987  6. School Transfers and Changes in Educational Objectives
 16988      The proposed rule discussed several examples of fraudulent ``pay-
 16989  to-stay'' schemes in which students were falsely reported as 
 16990  maintaining status in return for cash payments to DSOs.\339\ 
 16991  Furthermore, the D/S framework has enabled some aliens to become 
 16992  ``professional students'' who spend years enrolled in programs at the 
 16993  same educational level (for example, multiple associate degree 
 16994  programs) or complete programs at one educational level and enroll in 
 16995  lower educational levels (such as completing a master's degree and then 
 16996  enrolling in an associate program).\340\ While admission for a fixed 
 16997  time period will help to address these concerns, DHS proposed 
 16998  limitations on program changes within and between educational levels to 
 16999  further strengthen the integrity of the F nonimmigrant visa 
 17000  classification by better ensuring that aliens are in the United States 
 17001  primarily to study, rather than to reside permanently in the United 
 17002  States. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i). The final rule retains this 
 17003  provision.
 17004  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 17005  
 17006      \339\ 90 FR at 42094-95 (Aug. 28, 2025).
 17007      \340\ DHS analysis of data in SEVIS and valid as of May 7, 2025, 
 17008  and June 2, 2026.
 17009  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 17010  
 17011      DHS also proposed to retain some of the current school transfer and 
 17012  change of educational level conditions. First, as is the case 
 17013  currently, aliens would need to begin classes at the transfer school or 
 17014  program within 5 months of transferring out of the current school or 
 17015  within 5 months of the program completion date on his or her current 
 17016  Form I-20; and second, if the alien is authorized to engage in post-
 17017  completion or STEM OPT, he or she must be able to begin or resume 
 17018  classes within 5 months of transferring out of the school that 
 17019  recommended OPT or the date the OPT authorization ends, whichever is 
 17020  earlier. This is retained in this final rule, although, as compared the 
 17021  NPRM, the regulatory text in the final rule replaces the statement that 
 17022  the F-1 student ``must be able to resume classes within 5 months. . .'' 
 17023  with the F-1 student ``must be able to begin or resume classes within 5 
 17024  months . . .''. See new CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(G) and (H).
 17025      DHS retained the current provisions at 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i), 
 17026  rendering aliens who do not pursue a full course of study ineligible to 
 17027  change programs or transfer schools, and clarifying that failure to 
 17028  pursue a full course of study includes, but is not limited to, a 
 17029  student whose pattern of behavior demonstrates a repeated inability or 
 17030  unwillingness to complete his or her course of study. Just as delays 
 17031  caused by unacceptable patterns of behavior, academic probation or 
 17032  suspension are not acceptable reasons for program extensions and 
 17033  corresponding EOS of a student's current program, neither are they an 
 17034  acceptable reason for failing to carry a full course load. Such aliens 
 17035  will have failed to maintain F status, are ineligible for a change of 
 17036  program and school transfers and will be required to file for a 
 17037  reinstatement of status, if eligible. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i).
 17038      To complete a transfer, an F-1 student must first notify the 
 17039  student's current school (the ``transfer-out school'') of the intent to 
 17040  transfer and indicate the school to which the student intends to 
 17041  transfer (the ``transfer-in school''). Upon notification by the 
 17042  student, the transfer-out school will update the student's record in 
 17043  SEVIS as a ``transfer-out'' and indicate the transfer-in school and a 
 17044  release date. The release date will be the current semester or session 
 17045  completion date, or the date of expected transfer if earlier than the 
 17046  completion date of the established academic cycle. The transfer-out 
 17047  school will retain control over the student's record in SEVIS until the 
 17048  student completes the current term or reaches a release date, whichever 
 17049  is earlier. At the request of the student, the DSO of the current 
 17050  school may cancel the transfer request at any time prior to the release 
 17051  date. As of the release date specified by the current DSO, the 
 17052  transfer-in school will be granted full access to the student's SEVIS 
 17053  record and will then become responsible for that student. The student 
 17054  should then obtain a valid Form I-20 or successor form from the 
 17055  transfer-in school. This language is consistent with the proposal in 
 17056  the NPRM, but has minor clarifying edits. See new 8 CFR 
 17057  214.2(f)(8)(ii).
 17058      DHS has also retained this proposal to clarify to the public that a 
 17059  change to a higher education level can be accomplished in accordance 
 17060  with the transfer procedures outlined in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(ii). See new 
 17061  8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(iii).
 17062      Finally, DHS proposed technical updates. If the new program to 
 17063  which the student changes or transfers will not be completed within the 
 17064  authorized admission period established in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), then,

 17069  program end date, and would need to provide biometrics as authorized by 
 17070  8 CFR 103.16, if required. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(iv).

 17530  I. Change of Status
 17531  
 17532      The final rule retains, unchanged, the two provisions added to 8 
 17533  CFR part 248, which governs changes of status. In the first provision, 
 17534  DHS clarified that aliens who were granted a change to F or J status, 
 17535  before the effective date of the final rule, and are applying for 
 17536  admission as an F or J after the final rule's effective date may be 
 17537  admitted up to the program end date as noted on the Form I-20 or DS-
 17538  2019 not to exceed 4 years, plus a period of 30 days following their 
 17539  program end date, to prepare for departure or to otherwise seek to 
 17540  obtain lawful authorization to remain in the United States. See new 8 
 17541  CFR 248.1(e). CBP may admit these aliens into the United States up to 
 17542  the program end date, on the Form I-20 or DS-2019 that accompanied the 
 17543  approved change of status prior to the alien's departure, plus an 
 17544  additional 30 days, thus ensuring that they do not get more time than 
 17545  allocated by their program end date, since these F and J nonimmigrants 
 17546  would have received an admission period for D/S on the I-94 that 
 17547  accompanied the change of status approval.
 17548      The second provision, retained in the final rule, codifies the 
 17549  long-standing policy that, when an alien timely files an application to 
 17550  change to another nonimmigrant status, including F or J status, but 
 17551  departs the United States while the application is pending, USCIS will 
 17552  consider the application abandoned. Under section 248 of the INA, DHS 
 17553  may authorize a change of status to a nonimmigrant who, among other 
 17554  things, continues to maintain his or her status. Thus, pursuant to a 
 17555  policy that has been in place for decades, the change of status 
 17556  application of an alien who travels outside of the United States during 
 17557  the pendency of his or her request for a change of status is deemed 
 17558  abandoned. See new 8 CFR 248.1(f). Note, however, if there is an 
 17559  underlying petition filed along with the change of status, the petition 
 17560  may still be approved, but the alien generally would have to obtain the 
 17561  necessary visa at a U.S. Embassy or Consulate abroad before applying 
 17562  for admission to the United States in the new nonimmigrant 
 17563  classification.
 17564  
 17565  J. Classes of Aliens Authorized To Accept Employment
 17566  
 17567      DHS made the following updates to regulations pertaining to 
 17568  employment authorization: First, DHS struck the reference to D/S and 
 17569  updated the reference to 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vi) in 8 CFR 
 17570  274a.12(b)(6)(v). Second, in 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(10), DHS cross referenced 
 17571  language in 8 CFR 214.2(i) for I nonimmigrants, which clarifies that 
 17572  limitations currently in the provision (stating that an alien in this 
 17573  status may be employed only for the sponsoring foreign news agency or 
 17574  bureau) allow for freelance and self-employment situations where the I 
 17575  nonimmigrant may not have a ``sponsoring'' foreign news agency or 
 17576  bureau, and instead will need to show, among other requirements 
 17577  indicated in 8 CFR 214.2(i), that they are working for a qualifying 
 17578  foreign media organization.
 17579  
 17580  K. Severability
 17581  
 17582      In the event a provision in the section is not implemented, DHS has 
 17583  added severability clauses to ensure that the remaining provisions be 
 17584  implemented as an independent rule. The changes impact provisions that

**Analyzing Public Comments**

I'm incredibly excited! My recent focus has been on extracting valuable insights from public comments, and I've already uncovered some gems. I'm now leveraging `fr_grep` on a specific file, `2026-14439`, to pinpoint comment responses in Section IV that directly address the tricky edge cases. Let's list the relevant catches!


**Pinpointing Fee Information**

I'm now zeroing in on specific topics within the document `2026-14439`. My current task involves grepping for information about the costs and processing times associated with the I-539 form extension of stay. I'm focusing particularly on Section IV, and intend to identify all responses related to fees, costs, and processing times.


**Investigating Timing Requirements**

I'm now diving deeper into the nuances of filing deadlines. Specifically, I'm using `fr_grep` on `2026-14439` to search for mentions of "March 18" in conjunction with "six months" or "6 months". I'm also attempting to resolve a complex question regarding the 60-day departure period for D/S transition students and its impact on timely I-539 filings, and employment authorizations. To this end, I'm grepping for terms like "60-day," "transition," "EOS," "timely filing," and "employment." Moreover, I have started analyzing the key provisions of `8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(C)` in connection with `2026-14439`.


**Examining SEVP Requirements**

I'm now deeply engaged with the specifics of 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(C) again, specifically regarding F-1 students changing objectives or transferring, and the associated SEVP requirements. I'm taking another look at section 19004 of `2026-14439`, focusing on clauses (A) through (D) and their implications for maintaining status, transferring, and pursuing graduate studies.


**Clarifying Legal Provisions**

I'm now honing in on the regulatory text itself. Specifically, I'm examining a critical question related to an F-1 student's ability to transfer and change objectives, focusing on the tension in the rules, especially under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A). I've revisited Q5, which I think is a great example of this tension. I'm investigating how different interpretations might lead to conflicting conclusions, and thinking about how to frame this for you. I'm taking another look at the regulatory language, in connection with section 19004 of the document, especially at clauses (A) through (D) and their implications for maintaining status, transferring, and pursuing graduate studies.


**Interpreting Regulatory Text**

I'm now carefully examining the implications of 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(B) in relation to 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i). I'm focusing on the requirement that an F-1 student "who has completed a program" can change educational objectives or transfer, but with additional restrictions, including the significant exception in (C) that pertains to graduate-level studies. I'm especially interested in the specific conditions and potential SEVP authorization related to (C) that permits an exception.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

content.text:
**Analyzing Graduate Education Impacts**

I'm currently focused on the implications for graduate education. Specifically, I'm examining how the rule might disrupt common practices, like promoting master's students to Ph.D. programs mid-study. Line 8480, referencing "FR page 45042", clearly highlights this concern. The impact on Ph.D. students receiving master's degrees en route is also key. I am continuing to analyze associated points.


**Examining EOS Implications**

I'm now deeply immersed in the nuances of End of Status (EOS) applications, particularly in relation to program lengths and extensions. Line 8178, referencing "FR page 45039", is under intense scrutiny regarding implications for students in accredited 5-year programs. Furthermore, I've identified several sections (IV.G, VI.A, VI.F) and lines (13556, 17706) for I-539 fees, costs, and processing times. The next step involves a comprehensive grep to capture all relevant dollar figures and processing time mentions. Also considering Section IV.J concerning English language training.

  8470      Comments: Commenters stated that changes to graduate programs do 
  8471  not account for actual experiences of students. The majority of 
  8472  commenters expressed opposition to the proposed rule's prohibition on 
  8473  F-1 graduate students changing programs or educational objectives 
  8474  during their program of study. Commenters expressed particular concern 
  8475  about the impact on Ph.D. students, remarking that the proposed 
  8476  restrictions demonstrate a lack of understanding about the nature of 
  8477  graduate education, which often involves interdisciplinary work and 
  8478  evolving research interests.
  8479      Commenters stated that the rule would disrupt common practices in 
  8480  graduate education, including master's students being promoted to Ph.D. 
  8481  programs midway through their studies, Ph.D. students receiving 
  8482  master's degrees enroute to their doctorate, and students pursuing dual 
  8483  degrees at the graduate level. Another commenter expressed the proposed 
  8484  rule would eliminate the ``master-out'' option for Ph.D. students who 
  8485  are awarded a master's degree when they cannot finish, and harm 
  8486  ``academic mobility'' for second master's degrees and master's-out 
  8487  pathways. Commenters clarified that graduate school, particularly at 
  8488  the doctoral level, is not a fixed, linear path, and intellectual 
  8489  discovery often leads students to pivot to related fields. Commenters 
  8490  stated that the rule would punish academic growth by causing students 
  8491  to abandon years of work rather than transition programs. Many 
  8492  commenters expressed concern with the proposed rule's different 
  8493  provisions for graduate students compared to undergraduate students, 
  8494  noting that the proposed rule lacks explanation or rationale for these 
  8495  distinctions. One commenter reported extenuating and uncontrollable 
  8496  circumstances may cause a graduate student to transfer programs or 
  8497  institutions, while another commenter thought the proposed rule would 
  8498  punish students for issues beyond their control by locking students 
  8499  into a major their first year and by requiring graduate students to 
  8500  remain in their program. Another commenter stated that the proposed 
  8501  rule would make Ph.D. enrollment riskier and would leave open teaching 
  8502  assistant and research positions that are dependent on foreign 
  8503  students.
  8504      Commenters provided numerous reasons why graduate students might 
  8505  need to change programs, including refined research direction, changes 
  8506  in advisors, moves from master's to doctoral programs, suggestions from 
  8507  faculty members, personal or academic circumstances, and changes in 
  8508  research funding. Commenters emphasized the critical relationship 
  8509  between graduate students and their faculty advisors, explaining that 
  8510  students often choose specific institutions because of faculty members 
  8511  whose research aligns with their interests, reasoning that when faculty 
  8512  members relocate to another university, graduate students may need to 
  8513  transfer to continue working with their chosen mentors and maintain 
  8514  access to specialized research facilities. Commenters noted that 
  8515  research funding is often tied to specific faculty members, requiring 
  8516  students to follow their advisors to maintain financial support.
  8517      Commenters urged DHS to reconsider its restrictions on graduate 
  8518  students seeking to transfer or change educational objectives, with 
  8519  specific requests to allow Ph.D. students the option to transfer, 
  8520  particularly in cases involving academic or financial necessity. If DHS 
  8521  proceeds with finalizing the rule, commenters suggested establishing 
  8522  exceptions, such as allowing students to transfer to continue 
  8523  mentorship with their advisor, and proposed simplifying procedures for 
  8524  program extensions and transfers, especially at the graduate level. 
  8525  Commenters asked what happens after the 240-day authorized stay ends 
  8526  while an application is pending, the earliest filing date for 
  8527  applications, and how Ph.D. students whose programs exceed four years 
  8528  would justify extensions.
  8529      Commenters noted the rule could prevent individuals who completed a 
  8530  Ph.D. from later enrolling in a U.S. MD program or vice versa, despite 
  8531  these degrees preparing students for distinct career paths. Commenters 
  8532  expressed concern about uncertainty for medical residents on F-1 visas 
  8533  regarding whether residency would be considered a higher education 
  8534  level than medical school, potential barriers to changing disciplines 
  8535  during residency, and disruptions to transitions between PharmD 
  8536  programs or movement from PharmD to research-focused graduate programs.
  8537      Relatedly, a few commenters noted that the changes would prohibit 
  8538  students from pursuing a second master's degree which could hamper 
  8539  their ability to shift careers and add interdisciplinary training. One 
  8540  commenter pursuing a second STEM master's degree also expressed concern 
  8541  for the uncertainty surrounding using OPT after a second master's 
  8542  degree and stated that this might direct students away from the United 
  8543  States. Another commenter spoke about how the inability to pursue a 
  8544  second master's degree may hamper a student from ``applied, industry-
  8545  ready training.''
  8546      Response: DHS acknowledges that students may seek to engage in 
  8547  programs simultaneously at a lower level or obtain multiple degrees, at 
  8548  differing levels, throughout the course of their time in the United 
  8549  States. Students will be able to continue earning such credentials 
  8550  while also making progress in the degree program for which they have 
  8551  been issued a Form I-20. For example, a student issued a Form I-20 for

  8553  master's degree incidental to

  8569  academic growth of students. DHS recognizes academic pathways can be 
  8570  complex and that students may pursue multiple degrees or transition 
  8571  programs, including from undergraduate to graduate studies. The 
  8572  Department does not intend to discourage academic advancement or 
  8573  require students to abandon years of work.
  8574      DHS also recognizes the different approaches for undergraduate 
  8575  students and graduate students. This rule aims to balance program 
  8576  integrity and national security with the need to support legitimate 
  8577  educational pursuits. DHS believes differing approaches for 
  8578  undergraduate and graduate students are appropriate given the 
  8579  difference in the general ages of the students, a graduate student's 
  8580  previous opportunities to explore academic interests prior to entering 
  8581  graduate school, and a focus on more specific degree programs at the 
  8582  graduate level. DHS maintains it is appropriate to prohibit an F-1 
  8583  student at the graduate degree level or above from changing educational 
  8584  objectives at any point during their program of study for the reasons 
  8585  outlined above. However, DHS recognizes that extenuating circumstances, 
  8586  such as a school closure or a school's prolonged inability to hold in-
  8587  person classes due to a natural disaster, may prevent a graduate 
  8588  student from being able to continue their studies unless the student 
  8589  transfers to another SEVP-certified institution. The NPRM proposed 
  8590  prohibiting an F-1 student at the graduate level from transferring, 
  8591  without exception. DHS agrees with commenters that these situations may 
  8592  be outside the students' control and, taking this into consideration, 
  8593  DHS has amended the regulatory text to allow SEVP to authorize an 
  8594  exception to this transfer prohibition in extenuating circumstances. 
  8595  See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A), 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(C), and 8 CFR 
  8596  214.2(f)(8)(i)(D). For the purposes of this rule, ``extenuating 
  8597  circumstances'' for a transfer are rare, exceptional events beyond the 
  8598  control of the school and the affected students that prevent an SEVP-
  8599  certified school from continuing to provide the student's approved 
  8600  course of study, such as a permanent or extended school closure, a 
  8601  school merger that eliminates the student's program, a loss of 
  8602  necessary authorization for the school to enroll F-1 students, or the 
  8603  school's prolonged inability to deliver required instruction due to a 
  8604  natural disaster or comparable emergency. In such circumstances, SEVP 
  8605  may, in its discretion and in coordination with the impacted SEVP-
  8606  certified school or schools, permit the transfer of student records to 
  8607  another SEVP-certified school so that the student may continue, to the 
  8608  extent practicable, in the same educational objective. This exception 
  8609  is narrow, is intended only to preserve continuity of study in 
  8610  emergency situations, does not create an entitlement to transfer, and 
  8611  does not otherwise authorize an F-1 student to change educational 
  8612  objectives. Affected students generally will access this exception 
  8613  through their DSOs, as SEVP becomes aware of qualifying extenuating 
  8614  circumstances through notifications from SEVP-certified schools and 
  8615  SEVP's existing outreach to schools during such events.
  8616      Regarding the claim that the rule will make Ph.D. enrollment 
  8617  riskier and result in unfilled teaching assistant and research 
  8618  positions, DHS does not intend for this rule to significantly affect 
  8619  these populations since foreign students may still study, teach, and

  5694  underway to support the transition from D/S to fixed admission periods.

  5696  ensure a smooth transition and minimize disruption for students,

  5701  214.1(m) provide sufficient time for the rule's changes and that

content.text:
**Discovering Extenuating Circumstances**

I've struck gold with Q15! I found a treasure trove in Statement 4 regarding ELT and serious illness. Lines 8131–8134, from `91 FR 45039`, explicitly cover extenuating circumstances like illness, disability, and emergencies, maintaining student limits despite these hardships.


**Analyzing Program Extensions**

I'm now diving into extensions. The regulation `8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A)` confirms the 24-month admission limit for ELT students. However, the preamble, lines 16935-16938, emphasizes that the 4-year rule doesn't apply to language training. Statement 5 reveals accredited 5-year programs can continue, needing only an EOS application before the current period expires. This allows continued study while the application is pending, even if the program length exceeds the base duration.


**Clarifying Extension Eligibility**

I've hit a date discrepancy. The preamble mentions a six-month window from the rule's effective date, seemingly landing on March 15, 2027. Yet, the regulatory text at `8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i)` clearly states "on or before March 18, 2027" as the definitive deadline. This discrepancy needs clarification. Additionally, there appears to be a mistaken reference to September 15th within Section V.E.1 of `91 FR 45101`.

 17769  software updates as a direct result of the D/S rule. Training costs are

 17771  allocations and incur no additional cost to the U.S. taxpayer. The 
 17772  training for compliance with the rule will be part of regular training 
 17773  and training budgets and cannot be separated as a distinct cost.
 17774  Costs to Schools and Enrollments
 17775      The global market for nonimmigrant students is competitive and many 
 17776  U.S. schools hold an advantage over foreign institutions due to the 
 17777  quality of the programs they offer, however the final rule may have an 
 17778  impact on nonimmigrant student enrollment. The final rule affects only 
 17779  those F-1 and J-1 nonimmigrants who need additional time to complete 
 17780  their program or who wish to continue their education; however, DHS 
 17781  maintains that eligible students should have no difficulty with getting 
 17782  their EOS requests approved, which should alleviate concerns about the 
 17783  uncertainty of EOS approval. Schools may also incur costs for changes 
 17784  to their information systems and practices to implement processing 
 17785  under the proposed rule.
 17786      DHS expects this final rule will affect relatively few English 
 17787  language programs; the majority of ELT students were enrolled in 
 17788  programs shorter than 2 years. Some schools may choose to change their 
 17789  curriculum to be covered in a 2-year time period. It is possible that 
 17790  some language training programs would experience reduced enrollment due 
 17791  to the final rule.

 17793  participation of other J exchange visitors or I foreign information 
 17794  media representatives. Equivalent U.S.-based exchange visitor programs 
 17795  (outside of academia) may be more difficult to find in other countries, 
 17796  providing less of an incentive for nonimmigrants to choose an 
 17797  alternative.

**Analyzing Regulatory Impact**

I've shifted focus to thoroughly check every dollar figure within the Regulatory Impact Analysis section and relevant parts of Section VI of the document using `fr_grep`. I'm starting with the `2026-14439` document. I'm hoping to identify inconsistencies or important financial implications that were missed initially. This targeted approach feels more promising than a broader scan.

tools.name: fr_doc

content.text:
**Analyzing Q11 Regulations**

I'm incredibly excited about what the final rule for Q11 reveals! I'm delving into the nuances of rule `2026-14439`, focusing on its specific language (and omissions!) regarding extension of stay costs and USCIS decision timelines. Specifically, I'm analyzing the section on cost/fee.


**Investigating Fee Omissions**

I've uncovered a curious omission regarding the USCIS Form I-539 filing fee in the final rule. The regulatory text and DHS's preamble curiously don't specify the fee, instead referencing other documents. The only fee figures mentioned are those cited by commenters – $420, specifically from the online I-539 fee in the 2024 Fee Rule. This leaves one wondering, are they referencing an invalidated rule? I'll dig further.


**Examining DHS Statements**

I'm now focusing on the specific figures DHS presents in the final rule regarding Extension of Stay (EOS) costs and burdens, addressing Q11 directly. DHS highlights the requirement of separate filing fees for separate Form I-539s for F-2 dependents, versus a single fee when included via Form I-539A, from `91 FR 45013, 45110`. They present an average outside assistance cost of $490 (applied to 24.5% of applicants), and a 50-mile average round-trip for biometrics.


**Scrutinizing Time Burdens**

I'm now deeply engaged with the specifics within the PRA section (`91 FR 45120`). I'm dissecting the time burdens DHS presents per response: 1.667 hours for the paper I-539, 1 hour for e-filing, 0.35 hours for Supplement A, and 1.17 hours for biometrics. The total annual cost burden of $83,736,379 across all filings is eye-opening. I'm also cross-referencing this with the RIA summary's annualized EOS costs to nonimmigrants. Lastly, I will examine Section IV.G.2.a for any processing time data!

**Disclaimer:** I am an AI and cannot provide legal advice.


**Comparing Processing Times**

I'm now comparing the processing time information presented by DHS versus that provided by commenters. I'm noting the discrepancies – DHS offers general EAD processing times (60-120 days), encourages filing within 6 months, and acknowledges potential increases, while specific I-539 times are solely from commenters, citing 3.5 months, 6.5+ months, and sometimes exceeding 6 months. This contrast is key.


**Assessing Processing Data**

I'm now zeroing in on Q11 and the processing time estimates. I'm finding quite a range: 240 days to 18 months, with peak periods stretching from 12 to 18 months, or even 6 to 19 months. It seems like the commenters were spot on! This highlights how Ground Rule #2 is essential when dissecting Q11. I'm carefully double-checking premium processing data in Section IV.G.2.a as well.

    68                  By the President of the United States of America
    69  
    70                  A Proclamation
    71  
    72                  On September 19, 2025, Proclamation 10973 (Restriction 
    73                  on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers) (2025 
    74                  Proclamation), was issued to address significant abuses 
    75                  of the H-1B nonimmigrant visa program. The restrictions 
    76                  enacted by the 2025 Proclamation have proven to be 
    77                  highly effective but the underlying conditions 
    78                  necessitating the restrictions persist. It is therefore 
    79                  in the interests of the United States to extend the 
    80                  2025 Proclamation for an additional 12 months, until 
    81                  12:00 a.m. eastern daylight time on September 21, 2027.
    82  
    83                  As explained in the 2025 Proclamation, the H-1B 
    84                  nonimmigrant visa program was created to bring 
    85                  temporary workers in high-skilled functions into the 
    86                  United States, but it has been exploited to replace, 
    87                  not supplement, American workers with lower-paid labor. 
    88                  Certain employers, including information technology 
    89                  (IT) staffing and outsourcing firms, have abused the 
    90                  system to suppress wages and displace American workers, 
    91                  and this has both harmed the labor market for American 
    92                  workers while also making it difficult to attract and 
    93                  retain the most highly skilled temporary workers. IT 
    94                  staffing and outsourcing firms were found to supply a 
    95                  large volume of entry-level temporary H-1B workers, 
    96                  generally at a much lower salary compared to full-time, 
    97                  traditional workers, and some of these firms later 
    98                  outsourced IT roles to cheap labor markets overseas. 
    99                  This has led to a proliferation of lower-paid foreign 
   100                  labor flooding the American labor market and making it 
   101                  difficult for American workers and recent graduates, 
   102                  especially in science, technology, engineering, and 
   103                  math (STEM) fields, to find employment.
   104  
   105                  To combat these abuses, the 2025 Proclamation set forth 
   106                  a restriction on entry of certain H-1B nonimmigrant 
   107                  workers, except for those petitions that were 
   108                  accompanied or supplemented by a $100,000 payment, 
   109                  subject to very limited exceptions. The 2025 
   110                  Proclamation went into effect on September 21, 2025, 
   111                  and, since then, the $100,000 payment has been made for 
   112                  over 700 petitions.
   113  
   114                  Additionally, the 2025 Proclamation required initiation 
   115                  of rulemakings by the Department of Homeland Security 
   116                  (DHS) and the Department of Labor (DOL) to address 
   117                  systemic H-1B program concerns. On December 29, 2025, 
   118                  DHS published a final rule, titled Weighted Selection 
   119                  Process for Registrants and Petitioners Seeking to File 
   120                  Cap-Subject H-1B Petitions, 90 Fed. Reg. 60864 (DHS 
   121                  final rule), to address the policy goals consistent 
   122                  with section 4(b) of the 2025 Proclamation. Through 
   123                  this rule, DHS created and implemented a weighted 
   124                  selection process that prioritizes the allocation of 
   125                  visas to higher-skilled and higher-paid aliens to 
   126                  better protect the wages, working conditions, and job 
   127                  opportunities for American workers. This policy better 
   128                  serves the intent of the H-1B statutory scheme, 
   129                  incentivizes employers to recruit temporary workers for 
   130                  roles at the highest pay and skill levels, and was in 
   131                  effect for the Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 H-1B cap season. 
   132                  On March 27, 2026, DOL published a notice of proposed 
   133                  rulemaking, titled Improving Wage Protections for the 
   134                  Temporary and Permanent Employment of Certain Foreign 
   135                  Nationals in the United States, 91 Fed. Reg. 15454,
   136  
   137  [[Page 60498]]
   138  
   139                  to address the policy goals consistent with section 
   140                  4(a) of the 2025 Proclamation. The DOL's analysis of 
   141                  labor condition application data found that the average 
   142                  wage actually paid to H-1B workers, and the prevailing 
   143                  wage assigned to their positions, both remain well 
   144                  below the average wage earned by comparable American 
   145                  workers. The rule, once finalized, will better align 
   146                  prevailing wage levels with wages paid to similarly 
   147                  employed and located American workers and will 
   148                  strengthen overall program integrity. Finally, my 
   149                  Administration continues to explore other complementary 
   150                  efforts that would, among other things, reform the H-1B 
   151                  program and assist with cost-recovery for immigration 
   152                  program administration.
   153  
   154                  Since the effective date of the 2025 Proclamation and 
   155                  subsequent promulgation of the DHS final rule, there 
   156                  have been several measurable impacts on the H-1B 
   157                  program, including a significant reduction in H-1B 
   158                  registrations filed by large IT outsourcing firms, with 
   159                  the largest IT staffing and outsourcing firms reducing 
   160                  their combined H-1B registrations from 24,946 to 2,055, 
   161                  a 92 percent decrease. There has also been a large 
   162                  reduction in consular processing requests, which are 
   163                  used to bring workers into the United States, noting a 
   164                  nearly 97 percent decrease from the FY 2025 to FY 2027 
   165                  cap seasons. Finally, there has been a positive shift 
   166                  in FY 2027 H-1B registration and selection data toward 
   167                  higher-skilled and higher-paid workers, with 
   168                  registrations for beneficiaries with at least a U.S. 
   169                  Master's degree rising from 45.1 percent of total 
   170                  registrants for FY 2026 to 66.1 percent for FY 2027. 
   171                  Job offers with wages corresponding to the two highest 
   172                  wage levels accounted for approximately 46.3 percent of 
   173                  H-1B registration selections while those corresponding 
   174                  with the lowest wage level accounted for only 17.8 
   175                  percent. It is reasonable to conclude that the required 
   176                  $100,000 payment and newly implemented weighted 
   177                  selection process have had the combined effect of 
   178                  deterring low-wage and low-skilled recruitment while 
   179                  increasing access for high-skilled and high-wage 
   180                  workers, as intended by the 2025 Proclamation.
   181  
   182                  Although the 2025 Proclamation and subsequent 
   183                  rulemaking have had the desired effects, the underlying 
   184                  conditions precipitating their issuance persist and, 
   185                  without an extension of the 2025 Proclamation, it is 
   186                  highly likely that progress will halt and program abuse 
   187                  will resume, undermining American workers and posing a 
   188                  threat to the labor market that would be detrimental to 
   189                  the interests of the United States. The 2025 
   190                  Proclamation highlighted a number of concerns, 
   191                  including high unemployment rates for recent graduates, 
   192                  wage suppression, fraud, and national security threats. 
   193                  Currently, these issues continue to undermine our 
   194                  economy, with unemployment rates for recent college 
   195                  graduates standing at 5.7 percent as of June 2026, a 
   196                  marginal decrease from September 2025, when the rate 
   197                  was 5.8 percent. Underemployment for recent college 
   198                  graduates also continues to cause concern, having risen 
   199                  from 41.8 percent in September 2025 to 42 percent as of 
   200                  June 2026. Additionally, while DOL is actively in the 
   201                  process of promulgating a rule to restore integrity to 
   202                  the prevailing wage system, it will take a significant 
   203                  amount of time to correct and balance the labor market. 
   204                  Finally, while fraud and abuse continue to be 
   205                  identified and investigated, these are ongoing and 
   206                  pervasive concerns that require a sustained, 
   207                  comprehensive response reflected in the entry 
   208                  restriction imposed by the 2025 Proclamation.
   209  
   210                  A review of the 2025 Proclamation's impacts and other 
   211                  recent policy changes has shown significant measurable 
   212                  changes in H-1B filing patterns that demonstrate the 
   213                  effectiveness of the 2025 Proclamation and a need for 
   214                  its extension. An extension of the 2025 Proclamation 
   215                  will continue to protect the economic and national 
   216                  security interests of the United States, improve labor 
   217                  market access for American workers and graduates, and 
   218                  ensure that employers recruit only the most highly-
   219                  skilled and essential alien workers when needed in line 
   220                  with the original intent of the program. As a result, 
   221                  the Secretary of State, the Attorney General, the 
   222                  Secretary of Labor, and the Secretary of Homeland 
   223                  Security have jointly recommended an extension of the 
   224                  2025 Proclamation.
   225  
   226  [[Page 60499]]
   227  
   228                  As a result of these reviews and considerations, I have 
   229                  decided to continue to impose the limitations set forth 
   230                  in Proclamation 10973 on the entry into the United 
   231                  States by certain nonimmigrant workers. Accordingly, by 
   232                  the authority vested in me as President by the 
   233                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
   234                  America, it is hereby ordered:
   235  
   236                  Section 1. Restriction on Entry. (a) Pursuant to 
   237                  sections 212(f) and 215(a) of the Immigration and 
   238                  Nationality Act (INA) (8 U.S.C. 1182(f) and 1185(a)), 
   239                  the entry into the United States of aliens as 
   240                  nonimmigrants to perform services in a specialty 
   241                  occupation under section 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) of the INA 
   242                  (8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b)), is restricted, except 
   243                  for those aliens whose petitions are accompanied or 
   244                  supplemented by a payment of $100,000--subject to the 
   245                  exceptions set forth in subsection (c) of this section. 
   246                  This restriction shall expire, absent extension, 12 
   247                  months after the effective date of this proclamation, 
   248                  which shall be 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on 
   249                  September 21, 2026.
   250  
   251                      (b) The Secretary of Homeland Security shall 
   252                  restrict decisions on petitions not accompanied by a 
   253                  $100,000 payment for H-1B specialty occupation workers 
   254                  under section 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) of the INA, who are 
   255                  currently outside the United States, for 12 months 
   256                  following the effective date of this proclamation as 
   257                  set forth in subsection (a) of this section.
   258                      (c) The restriction imposed pursuant to subsections 
   259                  (a) and (b) of this section shall not apply to any 
   260                  individual alien, all aliens working for a company, or 
   261                  all aliens working in an industry, if the Secretary of 
   262                  Homeland Security determines, in the Secretary's 
   263                  discretion, that the hiring of such aliens to be 
   264                  employed as H-1B specialty occupation workers is in the 
   265                  national interest and does not pose a threat to the 
   266                  security or welfare of the United States.
   267  
   268                  Sec. 2. Compliance. (a) Employers shall, prior to 
   269                  filing an H-1B petition on behalf of an alien outside 
   270                  the United States, obtain and retain documentation 
   271                  showing that the payment described in section 1 of this 
   272                  proclamation has been made.
   273  
   274                      (b) The Secretary of State shall verify receipt of 
   275                  payment of the amount described in section 1 of this 
   276                  proclamation during the H-1B visa petition process and 
   277                  shall approve only those visa applications for which 
   278                  the filing employer has made the payment described in 
   279                  section 1 of this proclamation.
   280                      (c) The Department of State and the Department of 
   281                  Homeland Security shall coordinate to take all 
   282                  necessary and appropriate action to implement this 
   283                  proclamation and to deny entry to the United States to 
   284                  any H-1B nonimmigrant for whom the prospective employer 
   285                  has not made the payment described in section 1 of this 
   286                  proclamation.
   287  
   288                  Sec. 3. Scope and Implementation of Restriction on 
   289                  Entry. (a) The restriction on entry pursuant to section

    23                  Proclamation 10973 of September 19, 2025
    24  
    25                  
    26  Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant 
    27                  Workers
    28  
    29                  By the President of the United States of America
    30  
    31                  A Proclamation
    32  
    33                  The H-1B nonimmigrant visa program was created to bring 
    34                  temporary workers into the United States to perform 
    35                  additive, high-skilled functions, but it has been 
    36                  deliberately exploited to replace, rather than 
    37                  supplement, American workers with lower-paid, lower-
    38                  skilled labor. The large-scale replacement of American 
    39                  workers through systemic abuse of the program has 
    40                  undermined both our economic and national security. 
    41                  Some employers, using practices now widely adopted by 
    42                  entire sectors, have abused the H-1B statute and its 
    43                  regulations to artificially suppress wages, resulting 
    44                  in a disadvantageous labor market for American 
    45                  citizens, while at the same time making it more 
    46                  difficult to attract and retain the highest skilled 
    47                  subset of temporary workers, with the largest impact 
    48                  seen in critical science, technology, engineering, and 
    49                  math (STEM) fields.
    50  
    51                  The number of foreign STEM workers in the United States 
    52                  has more than doubled between 2000 and 2019, increasing 
    53                  from 1.2 million to almost 2.5 million, while overall 
    54                  STEM employment has only increased 44.5 percent during 
    55                  that time. Among computer and math occupations, the 
    56                  foreign share of the workforce grew from 17.7 percent 
    57                  in 2000 to 26.1 percent in 2019. And the key 
    58                  facilitator for this influx of foreign STEM labor has 
    59                  been the abuse of the H-1B visa.
    60  
    61                  Information technology (IT) firms in particular have 
    62                  prominently manipulated the H-1B system, significantly 
    63                  harming American workers in computer-related fields. 
    64                  The share of IT workers in the H-1B program grew from 
    65                  32 percent in Fiscal Year (FY) 2003 to an average of 
    66                  over 65 percent in the last 5 fiscal years. In 
    67                  addition, some of the most prolific H-1B employers are 
    68                  now consistently IT outsourcing companies. Using these 
    69                  H-1B-reliant IT outsourcing companies provides 
    70                  significant savings for employers: one study of tech 
    71                  workers showed a 36 percent discount for H-1B ``entry-
    72                  level'' positions as compared to full-time, traditional 
    73                  workers. To take advantage of artificially low labor 
    74                  costs incentivized by the program, companies close 
    75                  their IT divisions, fire their American staff, and 
    76                  outsource IT jobs to lower-paid foreign workers.
    77  
    78                  Further, the abuse of the H-1B visa program has made it 
    79                  even more challenging for college graduates trying to 
    80                  find IT jobs, allowing employers to hire foreign 
    81                  workers at a significant discount to American workers. 
    82                  These effects of abuse of H-1B visas have coincided 
    83                  with increasing challenges in the labor market in which 
    84                  H-1B workers serve. According to a study from the 
    85                  Federal Reserve Bank of New York, among college 
    86                  graduates ages 22 to 27, computer science and computer 
    87                  engineering majors are facing some of the highest 
    88                  unemployment rates in the country at 6.1 percent and 
    89                  7.5 percent, respectively--more than double the 
    90                  unemployment rates of recent biology and art history 
    91                  graduates. Recent data reveals that unemployment rates 
    92                  among workers in computer occupations jumped from an 
    93                  average of 1.98 percent in 2019 to 3.02 percent in 
    94                  2025.
    95  
    96                  Reports also indicate that many American tech companies 
    97                  have laid off their qualified and highly skilled 
    98                  American workers and simultaneously hired thousands of 
    99                  H-1B workers. One software company was approved
   100  
   101  [[Page 46028]]
   102  
   103                  for over 5,000 H-1B workers in FY 2025; around the same 
   104                  time, it announced a series of layoffs totaling more 
   105                  than 15,000 employees. Another IT firm was approved for 
   106                  nearly 1,700 H-1B workers in FY 2025; it announced it 
   107                  was laying off 2,400 American workers in Oregon in 
   108                  July. A third company has reduced its workforce by 
   109                  approximately 27,000 American workers since 2022, while 
   110                  being approved for over 25,000 H-1B workers since FY 
   111                  2022. A fourth company reportedly eliminated 1,000 jobs 
   112                  in February; it was approved for over 1,100 H-1B 
   113                  workers for FY 2025.
   114  
   115                  American IT workers have reported they were forced to 
   116                  train the foreign workers who were taking their jobs 
   117                  and to sign nondisclosure agreements about this 
   118                  indignity as a condition of receiving any form of 
   119                  severance. This suggests H-1B visas are not being used 
   120                  to fill occupational shortages or obtain highly skilled 
   121                  workers who are unavailable in the United States.
   122  
   123                  The high numbers of relatively low-wage workers in the 
   124                  H-1B program undercut the integrity of the program and 
   125                  are detrimental to American workers' wages and labor 
   126                  opportunities, especially at the entry level, in 
   127                  industries where such low-paid H-1B workers are 
   128                  concentrated. These abuses also prevent American 
   129                  employers in other industries from utilizing the H-1B 
   130                  program in the manner in which it was intended: to fill 
   131                  jobs for which highly skilled and educated American 
   132                  workers are unavailable.
   133  
   134                  The abuse of the H-1B program is also a national 
   135                  security threat. Domestic law enforcement agencies have 
   136                  identified and investigated H-1B-reliant outsourcing 
   137                  companies for engaging in visa fraud, conspiracy to 
   138                  launder money, conspiracy under the Racketeer 
   139                  Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, and other 
   140                  illicit activities to encourage foreign workers to come 
   141                  to the United States.
   142  
   143                  Further, abuses of the H-1B program present a national 
   144                  security threat by discouraging Americans from pursuing 
   145                  careers in science and technology, risking American 
   146                  leadership in these fields. A 2017 study showed that 
   147                  wages for American computer scientists would have been 
   148                  2.6 percent to 5.1 percent higher and employment in 
   149                  computer science for American workers would have been 
   150                  6.1 percent to 10.8 percent higher in 2001 absent the 
   151                  importation of foreign workers into the computer 
   152                  science field.
   153  
   154                  It is therefore necessary to impose higher costs on 
   155                  companies seeking to use the H-1B program in order to 
   156                  address the abuse of that program while still 
   157                  permitting companies to hire the best of the best 
   158                  temporary foreign workers.
   159  
   160                  The severe harms that the large-scale abuse of this 
   161                  program has inflicted on our economic and national 
   162                  security demands an immediate response. I therefore 
   163                  find that the unrestricted entry into the United States 
   164                  of certain foreign workers who are described in section 
   165                  1 of this proclamation would be detrimental to the 
   166                  interests of the United States because such entry would 
   167                  harm American workers, including by undercutting their 
   168                  wages.
   169  
   170                  Accordingly, by the authority vested in me as President 
   171                  by the Constitution and the laws of the United States 
   172                  of America, it is hereby ordered:
   173  
   174                  Section 1. Restriction on Entry. (a) Pursuant to 
   175                  sections 212(f) and 215(a) of the Immigration and 
   176                  Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. 1182(f) and 1185(a), 
   177                  the entry into the United States of aliens as 
   178                  nonimmigrants to perform services in a specialty 
   179                  occupation under section 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) of the 
   180                  INA, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b), is restricted, 
   181                  except for those aliens whose petitions are accompanied 
   182                  or supplemented by a payment of $100,000--subject to 
   183                  the exceptions set forth in subsection (c) of this 
   184                  section. This restriction shall expire, absent 
   185                  extension, 12 months after the effective date of this 
   186                  proclamation, which shall be 12:01 a.m. eastern 
   187                  daylight time on September 21, 2025.
   188  
   189                      (b) The Secretary of Homeland Security shall 
   190                  restrict decisions on petitions not accompanied by a 
   191                  $100,000 payment for H-1B specialty occupation workers 
   192                  under section 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) of the INA, who are 
   193                  currently outside the United States, for 12 months 
   194                  following the effective date of this
   195  
   196  [[Page 46029]]
   197  
   198                  proclamation as set forth in subsection (a) of this 
   199                  section. The Secretary of State shall also issue 
   200                  guidance, as necessary and to the extent permitted by 
   201                  law, to prevent misuse of B visas by alien 
   202                  beneficiaries of approved H-1B petitions that have an 
   203                  employment start date beginning prior to October 1, 
   204                  2026.
   205                      (c) The restriction imposed pursuant to subsections 
   206                  (a) and (b) of this section shall not apply to any 
   207                  individual alien, all aliens working for a company, or 
   208                  all aliens working in an industry, if the Secretary of 
   209                  Homeland Security determines, in the Secretary's 
   210                  discretion, that the hiring of such aliens to be 
   211                  employed as H-1B specialty occupation workers is in the 
   212                  national interest and does not pose a threat to the 
   213                  security or welfare of the United States.
   214  
   215                  Sec. 2. Compliance. (a) Employers shall, prior to 
   216                  filing an H-1B petition on behalf of an alien outside 
   217                  the United States, obtain and retain documentation 
   218                  showing that the payment described in section 1 of this 
   219                  proclamation has been made.
   220  
   221                      (b) The Secretary of State shall verify receipt of 
   222                  payment of the amount described in section 1 of this 
   223                  proclamation during the H-1B visa petition process and 
   224                  shall approve only those visa petitions for which the 
   225                  filing employer has made the payment described in 
   226                  section 1 of this proclamation.
   227                      (c) The Department of Homeland Security and the 
   228                  Department of State shall coordinate to take all 
   229                  necessary and appropriate action to implement this 
   230                  proclamation and to deny entry to the United States to 
   231                  any H-1B nonimmigrant for whom the prospective employer 
   232                  has not made the payment described in section 1 of this 
   233                  proclamation.
   234  
   235                  Sec. 3. Scope and Implementation of Restriction on 
   236                  Entry. (a) The restriction on entry pursuant to section 
   237                  1 of this proclamation shall apply only to aliens who 
   238                  enter or attempt to enter the United States after the 
   239                  effective date of this proclamation as set forth in 
   240                  section 1(a) of this proclamation.
   241  
   242                      (b) No later than 30 days following the completion 
   243                  of the H-1B lottery that immediately follows this 
   244                  proclamation, the Secretary of State, the Attorney 
   245                  General, the Secretary of Labor, and the Secretary of 
   246                  Homeland Security shall jointly submit to the 
   247                  President, through the Assistant to the President and 
   248                  Homeland Security Advisor, a recommendation on whether 
   249                  an extension or renewal of the restriction on entry 
   250                  pursuant to section 1 of this proclamation is in the 
   251                  interests of the United States.
   252  
   253                  Sec. 4. Amending the Prevailing Wage Levels. (a) The 
   254                  Secretary of Labor shall initiate a rulemaking to 
   255                  revise the prevailing wage levels to levels consistent 
   256                  with the policy goals of this proclamation consistent 
   257                  with section 212(n) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1182(n).
   258  
   259                      (b) The Secretary of Homeland Security shall 
   260                  initiate a rulemaking to prioritize the admission as 
   261                  nonimmigrants of high-skilled and high-paid aliens, 
   262                  consistent with sections 101, 212, and 214 of the INA, 
   263                  8 U.S.C. 1101, 1182, and 1184.
   264  
   265                  Sec. 5. General Provisions. (a) Nothing in this 
   266                  proclamation shall be construed to impair or otherwise 
   267                  affect:
   268  
   269  (i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or 
   270  the head thereof; or
   271  
   272  (ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget 
   273  relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals.
   274  
   275                      (b) This proclamation shall be implemented 
   276                  consistent with applicable law and subject to the 
   277                  availability of appropriations.
   278                      (c) This proclamation is not intended to, and does 
   279                  not, create any right or benefit, substantive or 
   280                  procedural, enforceable at law or in equity by any 
   281                  party against the United States, its departments, 
   282                  agencies, or entities, its officers, employees, or 
   283                  agents, or any other person.
   284  
   285  [[Page 46030]]
   286  
   287                  IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this 
   288                  nineteenth day of September, in the year of our Lord 
   289                  two thousand twenty-five, and of the Independence of 
   290                  the United States of America the two hundred and 
   291                  fiftieth.
   292
