    23                  Executive Order 14431 of September 18, 2026
    24  
    25                  
    26  Enhancing Program Integrity and Interagency 
    27                  Coordination in the Administration of the H-1B 
    28                  Nonimmigrant Visa Program
    29  
    30                  By the authority vested in me as President by the 
    31                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
    32                  America, it is hereby ordered:
    33  
    34                  Section 1. Purpose. The H-1B nonimmigrant visa program 
    35                  was created to identify uniquely skilled and highly 
    36                  specialized foreign temporary workers to strategically 
    37                  supplement the United States economy. Instead, the 
    38                  program has been widely abused by certain employers, 
    39                  third-party placement groups, and outsourcing firms to 
    40                  undercut and displace the supply of skilled United 
    41                  States labor. The large-scale, systematic abuse of the 
    42                  H-1B program to obtain non-qualifying foreign labor has 
    43                  undermined the additive purpose of the program and 
    44                  harmed the wages, working conditions, and job 
    45                  opportunities of skilled American workers.
    46  
    47                  The abuse of cheaper H-1B labor places downward 
    48                  pressure on domestic pay. H-1B visa holders earn far 
    49                  less than comparable United States-born workers, 
    50                  despite the statutory mandate that H-1B workers be paid 
    51                  equally to their domestic peers, with the estimated 
    52                  wage gap starting at $9,000 and climbing as high as 
    53                  $20,000 in H-1B reliant industries. One company even 
    54                  warned its shareholders that restrictions on cheap H-1B 
    55                  labor could force the company to use ``local'' workers, 
    56                  which ``may only be available at higher wages.''
    57  
    58                  Many employers have laid off large numbers of highly 
    59                  skilled American workers, only to promptly hire large 
    60                  numbers of H-1B workers who are often lower-skilled and 
    61                  lower-paid. For instance, technology sector employers 
    62                  have collectively requested H-1B visas for hundreds of 
    63                  thousands of workers, yet have also laid off somewhere 
    64                  between 800,000 to 1.3 million American employees from 
    65                  2022 through 2026. Employers have even forced laid off 
    66                  American workers to train their foreign replacements.
    67  
    68                  Many jobs held by H-1B workers eventually leave the 
    69                  United States entirely. Employers with outsourcing 
    70                  business models use teams of H-1B visa holders to 
    71                  replace United States workers at third-party client 
    72                  businesses and liaise with other individuals working 
    73                  off-site from their country of origin. As soon as 
    74                  practicable, much of their own work is transferred 
    75                  offshore. In Fiscal Year 2026, the top six users of the 
    76                  H-1B program operating with this outsourcing business 
    77                  model accounted for over 25,000 H-1B cap registrations. 
    78                  One foreign country's foreign minister even publicly 
    79                  admitted that H-1B ``has become the outsourcing visa.''
    80  
    81                  The systematic and organized abuse of the H-1B program 
    82                  is also a national security threat. Domestic law 
    83                  enforcement agencies have investigated H-1B-reliant 
    84                  outsourcing firms for engaging in visa fraud, 
    85                  conspiracy to launder money, and other illicit 
    86                  activities to encourage foreign workers to come to the 
    87                  United States. Abuses of the H-1B program also present 
    88                  a national security threat by discouraging Americans 
    89                  from pursuing careers in science and technology, 
    90                  risking vital United States leadership in these fields.
    91  
    92                  Numerous executive departments and agencies (agencies) 
    93                  have flagged employers' large-scale, systematic abuse 
    94                  of the H-1B program to obtain lower-paid, lower-skilled 
    95                  labor from abroad. These ongoing Government probes 
    96                  continue to identify widespread fraud and noncompliance 
    97                  among H-1B
    98  
    99  [[Page 60502]]
   100  
   101                  employers, such as: displacing American workers or 
   102                  otherwise giving preference to alien workers; 
   103                  misrepresenting the duties, requirements, or working 
   104                  conditions of job opportunities to avoid hiring or 
   105                  training American workers, falsely qualify jobs as 
   106                  specialty occupations, or lower applicable wage 
   107                  requirements; and misrepresenting aliens' 
   108                  qualifications to perform specialty occupations by 
   109                  submitting questionable foreign degrees from diploma 
   110                  mills as support for their H-1B visa applications. The 
   111                  pervasiveness of these violations and the persistence 
   112                  of the violators confirm that more needs to be done to 
   113                  preserve the H-1B program's integrity.
   114  
   115                  I have determined that continued efforts must be made 
   116                  to protect and prioritize the American workforce. It is 
   117                  therefore the policy of the United States that all 
   118                  relevant agencies shall implement appropriate measures 
   119                  to protect American workers from abuse of the H-1B 
   120                  program and ensure that the program serves the national 
   121                  interest.
   122  
   123                  Sec. 2. Interagency Coordination. When processing 
   124                  petitions, labor condition applications, and visas for 
   125                  the entry into the United States of aliens as 
   126                  nonimmigrants to perform services in a specialty 
   127                  occupation under section 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) of the 
   128                  Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) (8 U.S.C. 
   129                  1101(a)), the Secretary of State, the Secretary of 
   130                  Labor, and the Secretary of Homeland Security shall 
   131                  coordinate and consult with the Secretary of Commerce, 
   132                  the Secretary of Education, and the Administrator of 
   133                  the Small Business Administration to ensure the 
   134                  compliance of such petitions, applications, and visas 
   135                  with statutory requirements, including those in 
   136                  sections 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b), 212(n), 214(i), and 274B 
   137                  of the INA. The Secretary of Commerce, the Secretary of 
   138                  Education, and the Administrator of the Small Business 
   139                  Administration shall provide any relevant wage, 
   140                  employment, academic, industrial, or other economic 
   141                  information.
   142  
   143                  Sec. 3. Consideration of Applications, Petitions, and 
   144                  Visas. (a) Consistent with sections 
   145                  101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b), 212(n), 214(i), 215(a), and 274B 
   146                  of the INA, the Secretary of State, the Secretary of 
   147                  Labor, and the Secretary of Homeland Security shall 
   148                  take into account in any labor condition application, 
   149                  petition, visa, and entry of aliens entering or 
   150                  attempting to enter the United States as H-1B 
   151                  nonimmigrants to perform services in a specialty 
   152                  occupation whether the employer sponsor directly or 
   153                  indirectly engaged in layoffs within the previous year 
   154                  or plans future layoffs that negatively affect the 
   155                  employment of similarly situated United States workers.
   156  
   157                      (b) Within 30 days of the date of this order, the 
   158                  Secretary of Labor, through the Administrator of the 
   159                  Wage and Hour Division, shall begin reviewing data 
   160                  related to previously submitted labor condition 
   161                  applications to determine whether further action 
   162                  against sponsoring employers is warranted under section 
   163                  212(n)(2)(G).
   164                      (c) Pursuant to 3 U.S.C. 301, the authority granted 
   165                  to the President under section 215(a) of the INA is 
   166                  hereby delegated to the Secretary of State, the 
   167                  Secretary of Commerce, the Secretary of Labor, and the 
   168                  Secretary of Homeland Security to the extent necessary 
   169                  to implement this order, including the authority to 
   170                  issue or adopt rules, policies, operational guidance, 
   171                  or other guidance to carry out this order.
   172  
   173                  Sec. 4. General Provisions. (a) Nothing in this order 
   174                  shall be construed to impair or otherwise affect:
   175  
   176  (i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or 
   177  the head thereof; or
   178  
   179  (ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget 
   180  relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals.
   181  
   182                      (b) This order shall be implemented consistent with 
   183                  applicable law and subject to the availability of 
   184                  appropriations.
   185                      (c) This order is not intended to, and does not, 
   186                  create any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, 
   187                  enforceable at law or in equity by any party against 
   188                  the United States, its departments, agencies, or 
   189                  entities, its officers, employees, or agents, or any 
   190                  other person.
   191  
   192  [[Page 60503]]
   193  
   194                      (d) If any provision of this order, or the 
   195                  application of any provision to any person or 
   196                  circumstances, is held to be invalid, the remainder of 
   197                  this order and the application of any of its other 
   198                  provisions to any other persons or circumstances shall 
   199                  not be affected thereby.
   200                      (e) The costs for publication of this order shall 
   201                  be borne by the Department of Homeland Security.
   202                  
   203

  6010  regulation outlines the parameters for study, but students may make 
  6011  academic decisions within those parameters and continue to seek 
  6012  guidance from educational institutions, helping to protect the 
  6013  integrity of the F nonimmigrant classification while also preventing 
  6014  fraud and abuse. Furthermore, only DHS has authority to determine 
  6015  whether a nonimmigrant student remains in status. DHS believes, as 
  6016  discussed elsewhere in this rule, that nonimmigrant students will 
  6017  continue to come to the United States to study because of the quality 
  6018  of education offered and the ability to gain work experience in 
  6019  specialized fields.
  6020  (4) Financial Burdens
  6021      Comments: Commenters expressed significant concern about the 
  6022  financial burdens the proposed rule would impose on F, J, and I 
  6023  nonimmigrants, including increased fees for EOS applications and 
  6024  potential legal fees. Commenters noted that these costs would be 
  6025  particularly burdensome for students with limited financial resources 
  6026  and could accumulate over multiple extensions. Additional expenses 
  6027  could include travel costs for biometrics or interviews and indirect 
  6028  costs such as loss of income or health insurance due to pending EOS 
  6029  applications.
  6030      Response: DHS is authorized to charge fees for adjudication and 
  6031  naturalization services at a level to ensure recovery of the full costs 
  6032  of providing such services. DHS acknowledges that EOS applications will 
  6033  incur costs for nonimmigrants, but these costs are necessary for 
  6034  program integrity and national security. The Regulatory Impact Analysis 
  6035  accounts for these costs, and DHS believes the benefits outweigh the 
  6036  financial burden.
  6037  (5) Driver's Licenses
  6038      Comments: Commenters expressed concern about obtaining a driver's 
  6039  license and warned that the proposed rule would create additional 
  6040  complexities with respect to driver's licenses, as many states issue 
  6041  licenses only for the period of stay specified on a nonimmigrant's Form 
  6042  I-94. Affected nonimmigrants and their dependents would need to seek 
  6043  license renewal each time they file an EOS, adding further cost and 
  6044  inconvenience.
  6045      Response: DHS recognizes various state laws related to driver's 
  6046  licenses for aliens but does not have authority to adjust these state 
  6047  laws. DHS believes that timely filing of extension requests will 
  6048  minimize potential delays in license renewals.
  6049  (6) Emotional Burden
  6050      Comments: Many commenters described the stress, psychological 
  6051  impacts, and uncertainty F, J, and I nonimmigrants would face from 
  6052  dealing with the complexity of the extension process under the proposed 
  6053  rule. Commenters noted, for F nonimmigrants, this was especially true 
  6054  after investing significant resources in their education.
  6055      Response: DHS acknowledges that regulatory changes require 
  6056  adjustment and can be difficult. However, DHS believes the benefits of 
  6057  the rule outweigh these effects and that F, J, and I nonimmigrants will 
  6058  adapt to these changes. DHS declines to adjust the regulations for this 
  6059  reason.
  6060  (7) Economic Hardship and Special Student Relief (SSR)
  6061      Comments: A commenter supported codifying automatic extension of 
  6062  employment authorization for SSR beneficiaries with timely EOS 
  6063  applications, noting it aligns with longstanding policy and reduces 
  6064  lapses in employment. Others requested clarification on how automatic 
  6065  extension applies to severe economic hardship and raised concerns about 
  6066  increased administrative burdens.
  6067      Response: DHS appreciates the support and clarifies that 
  6068  individuals with a timely filed, pending EOS may receive automatic 
  6069  extensions of employment authorization under certain circumstances for 
  6070  up to 240 days or until the end date stated in a Federal Register 
  6071  notice. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii). The 240-day period is 
  6072  consistent with other nonimmigrant classifications and balances the 
  6073  need for oversight with minimizing disruptions. DHS acknowledges 
  6074  additional costs but believes the benefits outweigh the burdens.

  1536  activities, the collection of these fees remain essential in addressing 
  1537  the vulnerabilities of the OPT program for the reasons explained in 
  1538  this section. It is also conceivable that funds collected could later 
  1539  be effectively appropriated by Congress to various government agencies 
  1540  to further enhance the integrity of the immigration system. However, 
  1541  the deterrent nature of the OPT fee remains regardless of whether these 
  1542  funds are appropriated by Congress to government agencies for this 
  1543  purpose.
  1544      DHS considered some alternative regulatory approaches to address 
  1545  the issues in OPT that were discussed in sections IV.A. and IV.B. of 
  1546  the rule, such as applying STEM OPT requirements like site visits, 
  1547  training plans, and additional reporting to OPT more generally. 
  1548  However, DHS ultimately determined that proposing a fee for 
  1549  participation in the OPT program would offer an immediate and effective 
  1550  means to strengthen the integrity of OPT with minimal administrative 
  1551  burdens on the government. Unlike more complex regulatory alternatives, 
  1552  such as expanded site visits, increased reporting requirements, 
  1553  additional processes, and stricter procedural mandates, a fee can be 
  1554  implemented quickly and uniformly across all participants. This 
  1555  approach does not require DHS to deploy significant additional 
  1556  resources for enforcement or oversight. Moreover, the effect of a 
  1557  financial commitment is nearly immediate--those seeking to abuse the 
  1558  program are less likely to invest in participation when faced with a 
  1559  tangible cost, making engagement in OPT for nefarious purposes less 
  1560  attractive to bad actors. Furthermore, the financial commitment of this 
  1561  fee may encourage schools to apply a heightened level of scrutiny when 
  1562  reviewing an F-1 nonimmigrant student's request for OPT to ensure that 
  1563  the student is engaging in a legitimate OPT opportunity.
  1564      Although STEM OPT has regulatory safeguards, including reporting 
  1565  obligations, employer site visits, and the Form I-983 training plan 
  1566  requirement, DHS does not believe that simply extending those 
  1567  requirements to the initial period of post-completion OPT would be 
  1568  sufficient as an initial response to the overarching OPT program 
  1569  integrity concerns. Experience with STEM OPT indicates that additional 
  1570  procedural and documentation requirements, while useful, do not 
  1571  eliminate the risk of fraud, abuse, or noncompliance and may require 
  1572  substantial time and resources to implement, monitor, and enforce 
  1573  effectively. Solutions requiring self-attestations, reporting, or 
  1574  reliance on an honor system, without more, are insufficient to ensure 
  1575  the integrity of the OPT program. These mechanisms would need to be 
  1576  paired with enforcement activity, such as conducting more site visits 
  1577  across a broader range of employers, which may function less as a 
  1578  proactive fraud-prevention measure and more as reactive response to 
  1579  violations after they occur. In contrast, by requiring a financial 
  1580  commitment through an OPT fee, DHS would encourage participant to 
  1581  demonstrate a seriousness and genuine intent to comply with program 
  1582  requirements. The fee establishes a tangible stake in the process, 
  1583  helping to distinguish those who are committed to lawful participation 
  1584  from those who may seek to exploit the program. In addition to the 
  1585  current regulatory mechanisms in place, this additional layer of 
  1586  accountability supports the Department's broader efforts to uphold the 
  1587  integrity and effectiveness of the OPT program.
  1588      The Department recognizes the importance of restoring and 
  1589  maintaining public confidence in the OPT program through an immediate, 
  1590  effective regulatory solution, rather than a complex bureaucratic 
  1591  framework that may take years to yield results. By proposing a fee, 
  1592  rather than alternative administrative procedures, the Department seeks 
  1593  to minimize overregulation and complexities while responding to serious 
  1594  program integrity concerns that cannot be addressed quickly through 
  1595  such procedures alone. Recent concerns regarding misuse and fraud and 
  1596  the displacement of American workers have underscored the need for 
  1597  visible, effective action to reinforce the integrity of the program. 
  1598  The fee serves as a clear signal to the public and stakeholders that 
  1599  the Department is taking meaningful steps to safeguard the OPT program, 
  1600  while ensuring that legitimate participants continue to benefit from 
  1601  its opportunities.
  1602      DHS believes the OPT fee is a crucial first step to urgently 
  1603  address fraud, abuse, and noncompliance, in a targeted and immediately 
  1604  implementable manner. This measured approach allows for ongoing 
  1605  evaluation of the fee's impact and effectiveness, providing the agency 
  1606  with valuable data to inform future policy decisions. Importantly, the 
  1607  implementation of a fee should not be interpreted as precluding future 
  1608  changes to the OPT program through additional regulatory requirements; 
  1609  rather, it represents an immediate first step in a graduated strategy 
  1610  to address the urgent program integrity concerns. The Department seeks 
  1611  to retain flexibility to pursue additional regulatory measures in the 
  1612  future should further action be warranted.
  1613      In considering fees, DHS carefully evaluated various fee options, 
  1614  including exemptions to the fee for small educational institutions. See 
  1615  sec. VII.B.6. However, DHS estimates that 56 percent of regulated SEVP-
  1616  certified institutions are small entities. Id. This approach could 
  1617  leave significant fraud vulnerabilities unaddressed, given that many 
  1618  SEVP-certified institutions are small entities. Various factors and 
  1619  data were considered in this proposed rule, as explained in section 
  1620  VII.B.6.
  1621      Separately, DHS acknowledges that OPT is not the only practical 
  1622  training program with the potential for significant fraud and national 
  1623  security issues. Fraud and national security threats in CPT have also 
  1624  been historically prevalent and have increased along with the number of 
  1625  students engaging in CPT. DHS will continue to monitor these concerning 
  1626  trends within the CPT program and will take additional actions as 
  1627  necessary.
  1628  
  1629  D. Technical Edits
  1630  
  1631      The addition of an OPT fee under 8 CFR 214.13 would require 
  1632  clarifying that the other fees listed under the current regulations are 
  1633  solely in reference to SEVP fees, as evidenced by the section heading 
  1634  titled ``SEVIS fee for certain F, J, and M nonimmigrants.'' \118\ The 
  1635  proposed rule would add provisions regarding OPT fees under this 
  1636  section, such that it would be necessary to clarify which fees are 
  1637  specific SEVP fees and which are OPT fees.
  1638  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1639  
  1640      \118\ See 8 CFR 214.13 (current) (emphasis added).
  1641  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1642  
  1643  V. Discussion of Changes
  1644  
  1645  A. Establishing a Fee for Initial and Any Subsequent OPT
  1646  
  1647      The proposed rule would establish a fee of $70,000 per F-1 
  1648  nonimmigrant
  1649  
  1650  [[Page 64577]]
  1651  
  1652  student applicable to SEVP-certified schools that recommend an F-1 
  1653  nonimmigrant student to engage in OPT for the first time. See proposed 
  1654  8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii) and 214.13(i)(1). This fee amount would apply to 
  1655  any type of OPT that the student participates in for the first time 
  1656  (irrespective of whether it is pre-completion OPT or post-completion 
  1657  OPT). Id. The initial $70,000 is a one-time fee that an SEVP-certified 
  1658  educational institution must pay for each F-1 nonimmigrant student 
  1659  prior to a DSO's initial recommendation of an F-1 nonimmigrant student 
  1660  to participate in any type of OPT under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii) for the 
  1661  first time. To be clear, this OPT fee would not be tied to a specific 
  1662  employer; rather the OPT fee would be applicable when a school decides 
  1663  to recommend an F-1 nonimmigrant student for any type of OPT.
  1664      The proposed rule would also establish a fee of $30,000 per F-1 
  1665  nonimmigrant student applicable to SEVP-certified schools that make any 
  1666  subsequent OPT recommendation for an F-1 nonimmigrant student who has 
  1667  previously participated in OPT and has previously paid the initial OPT 
  1668  fee of $70,000. See proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2). As such, this 
  1669  subsequent $30,000 fee would apply to any type of OPT that an F-1 
  1670  nonimmigrant student participates in after having completed their 
  1671  initial OPT (regardless of whether it is another pre-completion OPT, 
  1672  post-completion OPT, or STEM OPT extension). Id. The OPT fee is not 
  1673  triggered by a change in employer but rather a school's decision to 
  1674  recommend a student for any type of OPT. For example, if an F-1 
  1675  nonimmigrant student obtains a DSO recommendation for pre-completion 
  1676  OPT and completes the training, they would need to obtain a subsequent 
  1677  DSO recommendation for post-completion OPT, regardless of whether the 
  1678  employer is the same for post-completion OPT and pre-completion OPT. In 
  1679  this instance, the school would need to pay $70,000 for the student's 
  1680  pre-completion OPT and $30,000 for the student's post-completion OPT. 
  1681  As with the initial OPT fee, the subsequent OPT fee would need to be 
  1682  paid for the F-1 nonimmigrant student prior to the DSO entering the OPT 
  1683  recommendation in SEVIS. See proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii). 
  1684  Additionally, USCIS would not grant employment authorization to any 
  1685  student prior to payment of the applicable OPT fee for the student. See 
  1686  proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(iii).
  1687      The proposed rule reiterates that the schools must pay the 
  1688  applicable OPT fees prior to the DSO entering the OPT recommendation 
  1689  for an F-1 nonimmigrant student in SEVIS. See proposed 8 CFR 
  1690  214.2(f)(11)(i)-(ii), 214.13(i). A DSO may not enter the OPT 
  1691  recommendation in SEVIS if the OPT fee has not yet been paid. The 
  1692  proposed rule requires the DSO to confirm that the school has paid the 
  1693  applicable OPT fee prior to updating SEVIS with the DSO's 
  1694  recommendation and before the student can apply to USCIS for employment 
  1695  authorization. See proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii)(B). The DSO would 
  1696  need to provide the F-1 nonimmigrant student with a new I-20 with the 
  1697  DSO's recommendation and OPT fee payment information so that the 
  1698  student may file the Form I-765 with USCIS. See proposed 8 CFR 
  1699  214.2(f)(11)(i), (ii)(C). The proposed rule provides that USCIS would 
  1700  not grant employment authorization to any student where the school has 
  1701  failed to pay the applicable OPT fee prior to issuing an OPT 
  1702  recommendation or in instances where the school has completely failed 
  1703  to pay the applicable OPT fees. See proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(iii).
  1704      For the initial OPT fees, the proposed rule provides that a school 
  1705  may request a refund if the F-1 nonimmigrant student has not received 
  1706  an employment authorization document for OPT for which the payment has 
  1707  been made. See proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1). The proposed rule makes 
  1708  clear that this fee would not be refunded under any circumstances once 
  1709  the F-1 nonimmigrant student has received an employment authorization 
  1710  document for OPT. Id. Similarly, for subsequent OPT fees, the proposed 
  1711  rule provides that a school may request refund if the student has not 
  1712  received an employment authorization document for OPT or an OPT 
  1713  extension. See proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2). The DSO would need to 
  1714  remove the F-1 nonimmigrant student's OPT recommendation in SEVIS 
  1715  before requesting a refund. For all refund requests, SEVP would review 
  1716  each request on a case-by-case basis and exercise discretion in 
  1717  adjudicating the request. See proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)-(2). The 
  1718  proposed rule also provides that SEVP may consider providing further 
  1719  guidance on its website regarding the refund request adjudication. Id. 
  1720  SEVP's determination on the refund request would be final and not 
  1721  appealable. Id.
  1722      DHS has also considered, as an alternative to the approach 
  1723  described above, having the one-time initial fee of $70,000 apply again 
  1724  to any initial period of OPT following the F-1 student's change to a 
  1725  higher educational level (e.g., to a post-bachelor's degree OPT and 
  1726  again to the student's master's degree OPT). DHS welcomes public 
  1727  comments on the rule in its entirety but especially encourages input 
  1728  from the public on this potential alternative.
  1729  
  1730  B. Technical Amendments
  1731  
  1732      Since an additional fee is being proposed within 8 CFR 214.13, DHS 
  1733  has also proposed some clarifying amendments to the current regulatory 
  1734  text to refer to a ``SEVIS fee'' rather than a ``fee.'' See proposed 8 
  1735  CFR 214.13(b), (e), (e)(1), (e)(3), (g)(3), and (h).
  1736  
  1737  C. Transition Period and Effective Date of the Final Rule
  1738  
  1739      To facilitate the transition, DHS is proposing that the final rule 
  1740  take effect 60 days after the date of publication of the final rule in 
  1741  the Federal Register (``effective date''), which would allow school 
  1742  officials, F-1 nonimmigrant students, and employers to prepare for 
  1743  changes in this fee rule. See proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3).
  1744      The OPT fee of $70,000 would start to apply for F-1 nonimmigrant 
  1745  students who will receive a DSO recommendation for any type of OPT that

  1747  8 CFR 214.13(i)(3). Thereafter, any subsequent DSO recommendations for 
  1748  OPT issued for any F-1 student who has previously participated in OPT, 
  1749  and for which the $70,000 OPT fee has been paid, will be subject to the 
  1750  subsequent OPT fee of $30,000 per alien. Id.

   196  that it determines may impact the privacy of an individual or is

   199      Docket: For access to the docket and to read background documents 
   200  or comments received, go to http://www.regulations.gov, referencing DHS 
   201  Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364. You may also sign up for email alerts on 
   202  the online docket to be notified when comments are posted or a final 
   203  rule is published.
   204  
   205  II. Executive Summary
   206  
   207  A. Purpose and Summary of the Regulatory Action
   208  
   209      The purpose of this proposed rule is to remove the availability of 
   210  the up to 60-day discretionary grace period from the regulations at 8 
   211  CFR 214.1(l)(2). The up to 60-day discretionary grace period 
   212  disconnects the alien's lawful status from the very basis of 
   213  eligibility under these employment-based nonimmigrant classifications. 
   214  By statute, an alien's lawful status in E-1, E-2, E-3, H-1B, H-1B1, L-
   215  1, O-1, or TN nonimmigrant classification is directly connected to and 
   216  contingent upon the alien conducting certain employment activities or 
   217  otherwise providing services in the United States that is generally 
   218  tied to a petitioning employer. In order for an alien in any one of 
   219  these classifications to maintain his or her status, the alien 
   220  generally must maintain the employment or continue to perform the 
   221  activity that was the basis of the alien's eligibility for the 
   222  classification and associated admission or grant of status. However, 
   223  under current regulations, these aliens, and their dependents, are not 
   224  considered to have failed to maintain nonimmigrant status for a grace 
   225  period of up to 60 days following cessation of the employment or 
   226  activity that was the basis of their nonimmigrant status, unless that 
   227  grace period is shortened or eliminated as a matter of DHS discretion. 
   228  Typically, the decision whether or not to shorten or eliminate the 
   229  grace period is made by DHS when a petitioner submits a petition on 
   230  behalf of an alien, or the alien submits an application on behalf of 
   231  him or herself, which seeks to extend the stay or change or adjust the 
   232  status of the alien following the cessation of employment or activity 
   233  that was the basis of his or her initial classification or grant of 
   234  status.
   235      The proposed rule, by removing the up to 60-day discretionary grace 
   236  period, would better align the regulations with the statutory 
   237  provisions governing the relevant classifications by requiring an alien 
   238  to depart from the United States immediately upon his or her failure to 
   239  maintain the employment or activity that was the basis for the 
   240  nonimmigrant classification or status (unless otherwise authorized to 
   241  lawfully remain in the United States). It would also reduce the 
   242  administrative burden on USCIS associated with the grace period.
   243      DHS originally extended this grace period to aliens in the listed 
   244  classifications, and their dependents, to encourage aliens who ceased 
   245  employment prior to the end of the petition validity period to remain 
   246  in the United States to pursue other immigration options to maintain a 
   247  lawful immigration status and, depending on the classification sought, 
   248  continue or regain employment authorization; and to help U.S. employers 
   249  to more easily facilitate changes in employment for existing and newly 
   250  recruited nonimmigrant workers.\1\ However, the relevant rulemaking did 
   251  not sufficiently consider the negative impacts of the grace period 
   252  provision. Upon reconsideration, and consistent with the Secretary of 
   253  Homeland Security's (Secretary) broad authority to set the time and 
   254  conditions of admission of nonimmigrants and to require that they

[cumulative 227 days through Aug. 31, 2028] + $13$ days in Sept. = **September 13, 2028** (or **August 14, 2028** if 240 days were measured from December 18, 2027 under the Form I-9 verification sentence of `(f)(5)(viii)`: $13$ Dec. + $31$ Jan. + $29$ Feb. + $31$ Mar. + $30$ Apr. + $31$ May + $30$ Jun. + $31$ Jul. = 226 + $14$ Aug.). **Crucially, however**, because **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)** makes this extension *'Subject to paragraphs (f)(9)(i)...'* (under which on-campus employment for a degree program ends at program completion), Tomás's RA authorization for this master's program cannot extend past his new program completion date of **May 19, 2028** (122 days after Jan. 17, 2028) unless he is transitioning to a new degree level or OPT. **(g) Authorized Stay If Approved; Obligation If Denied After I-94 Date:** **(1) If approved:** Under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi)** and **(f)(5)(v)** (and preamble **91 FR 45105**), his new stay runs through the new Form I-20 program end date (**May 19, 2028**) **plus 30 days**: $31 - 19 = 12$ remaining days in May + $18$ days in June = **June 18, 2028**. **(2) If denied after January 17, 2028:** Under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vii)**, there is no grace period—he **must immediately depart the United States** (and cease study/work; and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(i), (f)(7)(ii), (f)(7)(iii)(A)–(B), (f)(7)(vi)–(viii)** (**91 FR 45126–45127**). **Preamble Explanation (FR Doc. 2026-14439):** Section V.B (**91 FR 45098**), Section V.F.3 (**91 FR 45105**), Section V.F.4.b (**91 FR 45106–45107**), and Section V.F.5 (**91 FR 45108–45110**).","uncertainty":"There is a slight internal tension within **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)** (**91 FR 45125–45126**): Sentence 2 states the 240-day cap begins *'from the end date of his or her period of admission as indicated on the alien's Arrival/Departure Record, Form I-94'* (yielding September 13, 2028; For Tomás, both dates fall after his extended May 19, 2028 program end date, when on-campus RA eligibility for the program ends under `8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(i)`."},"Q4":{"answer":"**(a) Tomás's Travel (Dec. 22, 2027 – Jan. 5, 2028) While Form I-539 Is Pending:** **(1) Can he make this trip without putting the pending I-539 at risk, and does presentation at re-entry matter?** **Yes, he can travel without abandoning the I-539, and how he presents himself at re-entry matters decisively.** Because Tomás's previously authorized period of admission (his Form I-94 admit-until date of **January 17, 2028**) has **not expired** when he seeks readmission on **January 5, 2028**, final regulatory text at **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(B)** and **8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(i)–(ii)** sets out two distinct outcomes depending on what he requests at the port of entry: **(i) Re-entry for the balance of his existing admission period:** Under **8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(i)** (and **214.1(a)(4)(i)(B)**), if he seeks admission only for the unexpired balance of his previously authorized period of admission, **USCIS will NOT consider his timely filed Form I-539 abandoned**, and USCIS will continue adjudicating it. **(ii) Re-entry seeking a new full admission period on the updated Form I-20 (end date May 19, 2028):** Under **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(B)** and **8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii)**, if he instead seeks admission presenting his updated Form I-20 for a program end date beyond his previously authorized stay, CBP may admit him directly for the new period under `8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)` (through May 19, 2028 + 30 days = **June 18, 2028**), in which case **USCIS may deem his pending Form I-539 abandoned** as superfluous (preamble **91 FR 45098, 45100**)—though if CBP admits him through June 18, 2028, he achieves the extended stay at the port of entry without needing the I-539 (assuming he holds a valid F-1 visa; if relying on contiguous-territory/adjacent-island automatic visa revalidation with an expired visa under **8 CFR 214.1(b)(1)**, CBP may admit him *only* up to the unexpired prior stay). Preamble **91 FR 45100** also cautions that a traveling applicant must arrange to monitor and timely respond to any USCIS Request for Evidence (RFE) or risk denial for abandonment. **(2) What the rule says he should carry:** Under **8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(iii)**, he should travel with a copy of his **Form I-797C, Notice of Action** (or successor form) confirming USCIS receipt of his **Form I-539**, along with evidence of his proposed length of stay—specifically his valid **Form I-20** (plus standard entry documents required under **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)**: a valid passport and valid F-1 visa, if required). **(b) Travel While a *Change of Status* Application Is Pending:** Under final regulatory text at **8 CFR 248.1(f)** (added by **2026-14439**), if an alien timely files an application to change from F-1 to another nonimmigrant status and departs the United States while the application is pending, **USCIS will consider the change-of-status application abandoned**. As explained in preamble Section V.I (**91 FR 45115**), if an underlying nonimmigrant petition (e.g., Form I-129) was filed with the change-of-status request, the petition itself may still be approved, but the student generally must obtain the appropriate nonimmigrant visa at a U.S. embassy or consulate abroad and seek admission at a port of entry to assume the new status.","basis":"**Final Regulatory Text (FR Doc. 2026-14439):** **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(B)** (**91 FR 45122**); **8 CFR 214.1(b)(1)** (**91 FR 45122**); **8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(i)–(iii)** (**91 FR 45123**); and **8 CFR 248.1(f)** (**91 FR 45131**). **Preamble Explanation (FR Doc. 2026-14439):** Section V.B (**91 FR 45098**), Section V.C (**91 FR 45099**), Section V.D (**91 FR 45100**), and Section V.I (**91 FR 45115**).","uncertainty":"There is a minor drafting quirk in **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(B)** (**91 FR 45122**): when an F-1 student with a pending EOS seeks readmission for the balance of an unexpired stay, `(a)(4)(i)(B)` says CBP may admit the student *'up to the unexpired period of stay authorized prior to the alien's departure, plus an additional 30 days as provided in § 214.2(f)(5)(v)'*, even though Tomás's January 17, 2028 I-94 date *already* includes his 30-day departure period after December 18, 2027. Whether CBP admits him to January 17, 2028 or adds 30 days makes no difference to preserving his pending Form I-539 under **8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(i)**. In addition, the regulation does not explicitly address whether travel and readmission for the unexpired balance affects the 240-day automatic on-campus employment extension under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)**, though because `(c)(8)(i)` preserves the timely filed EOS un-abandoned, the predicate for `(f)(5)(viii)` remains intact."},"Q5":{"answer":"**Conclusion:** Under the most defensible, harmonized reading of the final rule (**2026-14439**), **yes, Mei's SEVIS record can be transferred from School A to School B once she completes her master's degree on May 14, 2027** (with a SEVIS transfer release after program completion and a Form I-539 EOS filed with USCIS on or before July 13, 2027)—**however**, there is a significant drafting tension in **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(C)** that creates operational risk if she attempts to transfer *before* May 14, 2027 or if DHS/SEVIS applies `(f)(8)(i)(C)` literally to post-completion graduate records. **Provisions Bearing on Mei and How Each Applies:** **(1) 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) (D/S transition stay and EOS requirement):** Because Mei is in the D/S transition group maintaining status on September 15, 2026, she is authorized to remain until her Form I-20 program end date (**May 14, 2027**) plus 60 days = **July 13, 2027** ($31 - 14 = 17$ days in May + $30$ in June + $13$ in July = 60 days), and to start her PhD on August 23, 2027 she must apply for an EOS with USCIS under `8 CFR 214.1(c)(2)` (unless she departs and re-enters through CBP). **(2) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i) (continuing F-1 students):** Expressly permits continuing F-1 students to be granted additional time to begin a new program of study under `(f)(5)(ii)(D)` and `(f)(7)` (and `(f)(8)(iv)`). **(3) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A) (graduate restriction *during* a program):** Bars an F-1 student at the graduate degree level or above from changing educational objectives *'at any point **during their program of study**'* and from transferring *'at any point **during their program of study**'* (absent an SEVP extenuating-circumstances exception, which preamble **91 FR 45043** limits to emergencies like school closure or natural disaster). Because Mei is finishing her master's on May 14, 2027 rather than transferring mid-program, `(f)(5)(ii)(A)`'s temporal limit (*'during their program of study'*) does not bar a post-completion move. **(4) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(B)–(D) (progression to higher educational level):** Paragraph `(B)` expressly provides that an F-1 student who *'has completed a program in the United States at one educational level and begins a new program at a **higher educational level** is considered to be maintaining F-1 status'* (Master's is level 6 and Doctorate/PhD is level 7 on SEVP's Form I-17 scale, preamble **91 FR 45043**), so `(C)`'s ban on same/lower-level programs does not apply, and `(D)` requires an EOS filing if needed. **(5) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(A)–(H) (transfer/level-change eligibility checklist):** Mei satisfies `(A)` (maintaining status through July 13, 2027), `(B)(2)` (*'Have completed a degree program'* as of May 14, 2027; `(B)(1)` before then), `(D)` (completed her first academic year at initial-I-20 issuer School A, having started Aug. 2025), `(E)`–`(F)` (no probation/suspension or pattern of non-completion), and `(G)` (PhD start date August 23, 2027 is within **5 months** of May 14, 2027—deadline October 14, 2027; `(H)` is inapplicable). **However, paragraph `(f)(8)(i)(C)` requires that *'The student is not currently in a graduate level program of study, unless an exception has been authorized by SEVP for extenuating circumstances under paragraph (f)(5)(ii)(A)'*.** Read in harmony with `(f)(5)(ii)(A)` (*'during their program'*), `(f)(5)(ii)(B)`, `(f)(8)(i)(B)(2)` (*'completed a degree program'*), and `(f)(8)(iii)`, once Mei completes her master's on May 14, 2027 and enters her 60-day departure period, she is no longer *'currently in'* a graduate program of study, allowing transfer; conversely, while still enrolled prior to May 14, 2027, she *is* 'currently in' a graduate program, and if SEVIS coded `(f)(8)(i)(C)` to block any transfer out of a graduate-level SEVIS record even post-completion, SEVIS transfer would be blocked (though Mei could still depart and re-enter with an initial PhD I-20 from School B on or after July 24, 2027—up to 30 days before Aug. 23, 2027—under **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)** and **214.2(f)(5)(ii)(B)**). **(6) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(ii)–(iv) (procedures and EOS):** Govern SEVIS release-date mechanics, confirm level changes follow transfer procedures, and require filing Form I-539 with School B's endorsed PhD I-20 before authorized stay expires (July 13, 2027). **Could Anything in the Rule or Later FR Documents Change This Conclusion?** **(i) In the rule:** **Yes**—under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E)**, until **September 14, 2028**, DHS may delay or suspend implementation of **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A)–(C)** via Federal Register and SEVP website notice if infeasible (e.g., SEVIS technical limitations), and DHS also stated in the preamble (**91 FR 45039, 45043**) it will issue stakeholder guidance on graduate pathways (and CRA review or severable judicial invalidation under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(20)** could also alter the rule). **(ii) In later FR documents:** **No** document published in the Federal Register through November 14, 2026 has delayed, suspended, or amended these provisions.","basis":"**Final Regulatory Text (FR Doc. 2026-14439):** **8 CFR 214.1(c)(2), (m)(1)** (**91 FR 45122–45123**); **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i), (f)(5)(ii)(A)–(E), (f)(7)(iii), (f)(8)(i)(A)–(H), (f)(8)(ii)–(iv), (f)(20)** (**91 FR 45124–45127**). **Preamble Explanation (FR Doc. 2026-14439):** `DATES` (**91 FR 44976**), Section IV.J.1.b & f–g (**91 FR 45038–45039, 45042–45044**), Section V.A (**91 FR 45097**), and Section V.F.2 & 6 (**91 FR 45103–45105, 45111**).","uncertainty":"**8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(C)** creates genuine textual ambiguity as to (1) whether a graduating master's student may notify School A *before* May 14, 2027 to schedule a May 14+ SEVIS release date under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(ii)** without being treated as 'currently in a graduate level program of study,' or must wait until May 15, 2027 (during her 60-day departure period) to request the transfer, and (2) how SEVIS software enforces `(f)(8)(i)(C)` for completed graduate records moving to a higher level under `(f)(5)(ii)(B)`. Additionally, **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E)** covers delaying `(f)(5)(ii)(A)–(C)` without expressly citing `(f)(8)(i)(C)`, though `(f)(8)(i)` cross-references `(f)(5)(ii)(A)–(D)`."},"Q6":{"answer":"**(a) Eligibility for F-1 Status for the MBA Under Either Route:** **No—Ahmed cannot obtain F-1 status for the MBA under either SEVIS transfer or travel and re-entry.** Final regulatory text at **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C)** (added by **2026-14439**) explicitly provides: *'An alien who has completed a program **after September 15, 2026**, in the United States as an F-1 student at one educational level **may not maintain, be admitted, or otherwise be provided F-1 status** through a program at the **same educational level** or a lower educational level.'* Because Ahmed completes his master's degree on **December 11, 2026** (which is after September 15, 2026) and an MBA is also at the **same educational level** (Master's, level 6 on SEVP's educational-level hierarchy, preamble **91 FR 45038, 45043**), **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C)** (together with **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(B)** and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)**, which conditions SEVIS transfer/level-change eligibility on maintaining status under `(f)(5)(ii)(A)–(D)`) bars him from both (1) maintaining F-1 status via SEVIS transfer/EOS and (2) departing and being admitted in F-1 status on a new initial Form I-20 (confirmed by preamble **91 FR 45104** & fn. 321). **(b) Transfer Timing Rule for an August 2027 Start:** Independently of the same-level bar in (a), **a SEVIS transfer is barred by the 5-month transfer timing limit in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(G)**, which requires the student to begin classes at the transfer school within **5 months** of transferring out of the current school or within **5 months** of the program completion date on his current Form I-20, whichever is earlier. *Date arithmetic:* December 11, 2026 + 5 months = **May 11, 2027** (and because he does not apply for OPT, **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(H)** does not apply). An **August 2027** start date is nearly 8 months after December 11, 2026—well past the **May 11, 2027** cutoff. **(c) Authorized Stay After Completing Master's (No Other Filings):** Assuming December 11, 2026 is the program end date on Ahmed's Form I-20 valid on September 15, 2026, under **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)** (D/S transition group) he may remain until his program end date **plus a 60-day departure period**: **February 9, 2027**. *Date arithmetic:* **December 11, 2026** + **60 days**: $31 - 11 = 20$ remaining days in December (to Dec. 31, 2026) + $31$ days in January 2027 (to Jan. 31, 2027, cumulative 51 days) + $9$ days in February ($60 - 51 = 9$) = **February 9, 2027**. **(d) Could the Answer to (a) Change Before August 2027?** **Yes, as to the leave-and-re-enter route (but NOT the SEVIS transfer route).** Under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E)**, at any time until **September 14, 2028**, DHS has discretionary authority to **delay or suspend implementation of 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A)–(C)**—including `(C)`'s ban on same-level F-1 programs—if DHS determines implementation is infeasible for any reason, by publishing a notification in the Federal Register and on SEVP's website (`studyinthestates.dhs.gov`). (CRA disapproval or judicial invalidation of `(f)(5)(ii)(C)` under severability clause **8 CFR 214.2(f)(20)** could have the same effect.) If `(f)(5)(ii)(C)` were suspended or invalidated before August 2027, Ahmed **could obtain F-1 status by departing and re-entering on a new initial MBA Form I-20**; however, **he still could NOT use a SEVIS transfer** for an August 2027 start because `(f)(5)(ii)(E)` does not authorize suspending the independent 5-month limit in **8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(G)** (and his D/S stay ends February 9, 2027).","basis":"**Final Regulatory Text (FR Doc. 2026-14439):** **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)** (**91 FR 45123**); **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(B)–(C), (E)** (**91 FR 45125**); **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)** (**91 FR DHS *does* state: that co-applicant F-2 dependents included via **Form I-539A** on the principal's Form I-539 require **only one filing fee**, whereas a separate Form I-539 requires a separate fee (**91 FR 45013, 45110**); an estimated average outside/legal assistance cost of **$490** for the **24.5%** of applicants assumed to use paid help (**91 FR 45083** & fn. 275); an average **50-mile** round trip for biometrics (**91 FR 45083**); PRA time-burden estimates of **1 hour** (Form I-539 e-file), **1.667 hours** (Form I-539 paper), **0.35 hours** (Supplement A / I-539A), and **1.17 hours** (biometrics), with **$83,736,379** total annual PRA cost burden across all I-539 respondents (**91 FR 45120**); and **$317.9 million** (3% discount) / **$317.3 million** (7% discount) in annualized EOS costs to nonimmigrants (**91 FR 45116**). **(iii) Commenter statements only (NOT DHS authority):** All specific per-filing fee figures in the rule appear solely in summaries of public comments—one commenter cited a **$420** filing fee (**91 FR 45055**) and another cited **~$1,680** for four EOS filings (**91 FR 45082**, i.e., $420 × 4), while others cited **$555** including biometrics (**91 FR 45065**), **$367 to over $800** (**91 FR 45056**), and **$750 to $3,000** for private legal counsel (**91 FR 45082**). **(2) How Long USCIS Takes to Decide Form I-539:** **(i) DHS preamble text:** DHS explicitly states that **DHS 'cannot guarantee processing times'**, that processing times are **'subject to change'**, and that the rule **'may cause an increase in USCIS processing times'** (**91 FR 45009, 45021, 45025, 45029, 45031, 45083–45084**), directing readers to USCIS's online Case Processing Times page (`https://egov.uscis.gov/processing-times/`, **91 FR 45084** fn. 277) and noting premium processing is not currently available for these EOS filings though DHS will continue to explore expanding it (**91 FR 45051–45052**). DHS states *EAD* (Form I-765) processing times are *'typically **60–120 days** for foreign students and **90–120 [days]** for most others'* (**91 FR 45032, 45107**), encourages filing EOS within **6 months (180 days)** before stay expires (**91 FR 45043, 45106–45107, 45110**), and provides up to **240 days** of automatic employment continuation while a timely EOS is pending (**8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)**). **(ii) Commenter statements only (NOT DHS authority):** Every specific Form I-539 processing-time number in the rule comes from commenters, who reported **~3.5 months** for extensions (and **4.5 months** for changes to F-1/J-1 at the California Service Center, **91 FR 44999, 45083**), **more than 6.5 months** for Service Center Operations to decide 80% of EOS requests (**91 FR 45063**), and ranges **often exceeding 240 days**, **6 to 19 months**, **12 to 18 months**, or **up to 18 months** during backlogs (**91 FR 45031, 45036, 45048, 45051**). **(3) Accurate Draft Handout Text (2 sentences):** *'To extend your F-1 stay in the United States, you must file Form I-539 with USCIS and pay the current Form I-539 filing fee listed on USCIS's fee schedule (one filing fee covers both you and any F-2 dependents included on Form I-539A, and biometrics may also be required). Under final regulatory text at **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)** (added by **2026-14439**), as a D/S transition student maintaining status on September 15, 2026, Priya is authorized to remain in F-1 status until her I-20 program end date (**May 15, 2027**) **plus a 60-day departure period** (through **July 14, 2027**). Under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)**, an EOS application is timely filed if USCIS's receipt date (`8 CFR 103.2(a)(7)`) is **on or before the date the authorized period of stay expires**, and preamble Section V.E.1 (**91 FR 45101**) explicitly confirms that D/S transition F-1 students may file an EOS request up to their program end date **plus the additional 60 days**. **(b) Does She Keep the Automatic Extension of On-Campus or CPT Employment If She Files During Those 60 Days?** **No.** If USCIS receives her Form I-539 after May 15, 2027 (during the 60-day departure period of May 16 – July 14, 2027), she may remain in the U.S. and continue studying, **but she receives NO automatic extension of on-campus or CPT employment** and must wait until USCIS approves the Form I-539 before engaging in employment or CPT. Three provisions establish this: **(1) 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)** explicitly provides that for D/S transition students, *'any authorized employment or training continues **until the program end date** on such F or J nonimmigrant's Form I-20'* (May 15, 2027)—meaning her underlying on-campus and CPT work authorization ends on May 15, 2027 and does not continue into the 60-day departure period; **(2) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)** and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)** bar any automatic extension of on-campus, CPT, or hardship employment when an EOS is filed during the post-program departure period (and note that CPT also cannot extend past the DSO-authorized CPT end date on Form I-20); and **(3)** for Form I-9 verification under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)**, Priya lacks an unexpired employment period (and lacks a fixed-date Form I-94) once May 15, 2027 passes. **Recommendation for the Adviser:** Advise Priya that **(1)** if she wants uninterrupted on-campus or CPT work authorization, her DSO must update SEVIS and **USCIS must receive her Form I-539 on or before May 15, 2027** (ideally up to 6 months early per DHS's recommendation at **91 FR 45106–45107, 45110**, so she also has her Form I-797C receipt notice in hand by May 15, 2027 for Form I-9 purposes); **(2)** if she is extending her *current* program, the DSO **must** enter the SEVIS extension on or before **May 15, 2027** regardless of when she files with USCIS, or else she falls out of status and needs reinstatement (**8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(viii)**); and **(3)** if she does not need summer work authorization (e.g., transferring to a fall master's program), while filing through **July 14, 2027** is timely under `214.1(m)(1)`, having USCIS receive the I-539 within the first 30 days (**on or before June 14, 2027**) is the safest practice to avoid any literal cross-reference friction with `214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)`'s reference to 'the 30-day period.'","basis":"**Final Regulatory Text (FR Doc. 2026-14439):** **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)** (**91 FR 45123**); Q1.answer: **(a) FR Document Number and Citation:** Federal Register Document Number **2026-14439**, titled *Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media*, published at **91 FR 44976**, with full page range **91 FR 44976–45131** (156 pages). **(b) Publication Date and Effective Date:** Published on **July 17, 2026**; effective on **September 15, 2026** (date arithmetic: July 17, 2026 + 60 days = 14 remaining days in July [31 - 17] + 31 days in August [45] + 15 days in September = September 15, 2026). **(c) Docket Number and RIN:** Docket **DHS Docket No. ICEB-2025-0001**; Regulation Identifier Number **RIN 1653-AA95**. **(d) Proposed Rule Finalized:** Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), FR Document Number **2025-16554**, published at **90 FR 42070** (page range **90 FR 42070–42115**), on **August 28, 2025**. **(e) Changes or Potential Changes to Effective Date:** As of November 14, 2026, **nothing in the Federal Register has changed, delayed, or terminated** the rule's September 15, 2026 effective date. However, two mechanisms described in the rule bear on potential changes: **(1) Congressional Review Act (CRA) review:** Because the rule is classified as a 'major rule' under 5 U.S.C. 804, its effective date is governed by the CRA (at least 60 days after Congress receives DHS's CRA report or 60 days after FR publication, whichever is later), and DHS expressly states in the `DATES` caption that if congressional review changes the effective date or terminates the rule, DHS will publish a document in the Federal Register establishing the actual effective date or termination; because CRA review runs by congressional session/legislative days rather than calendar days, congressional disapproval could still occur if the CRA review window remains open. **(2) Targeted sub-provision suspension/delay (distinct from the rule's overall effective date):** Under final regulatory text at **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E)**, DHS retains discretionary authority until **September 14, 2028** to delay or suspend implementation of the school-transfer and educational-objective restrictions in **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A)–(C)** via Federal Register notification (none has been published as of November 14, 2026). Judicial invalidation of specific provisions is also contemplated by severability clauses (**8 CFR 214.1(m)(4)**; **8 CFR 214.2(f)(20), (i)(8), (j)(6)**).
