Q11.answer: **What the Final Rule (2026-14439) Actually Says—Separating Authority from Commenter Statements:** **(1) Cost of an Extension of Stay (Form I-539):** **(i) Final regulatory text:** **Does NOT state a dollar filing fee**; **8 CFR 214.1(c)(2)** and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A), (iv)** (**91 FR 45122–45123, 45126**) require submitting the USCIS-designated form with *'the required fees'* / *'the appropriate fee'* per form instructions and appearing for any biometrics required under `8 CFR 103.16`. **(ii) DHS preamble / PRA / RIA text:** DHS itself **never states the current per-application Form I-539 filing fee** in the Federal Register text (instead referring readers to Table 16 of the docketed Regulatory Impact Analysis at **91 FR 45082**, and in fn. 276 at **91 FR 45083** citing only the enjoined 2020 Fee Rule). DHS *does* state: that co-applicant F-2 dependents included via **Form I-539A** on the principal's Form I-539 require **only one filing fee**, whereas a separate Form I-539 requires a separate fee (**91 FR 45013, 45110**); an estimated average outside/legal assistance cost of **$490** for the **24.5%** of applicants assumed to use paid help (**91 FR 45083** & fn. 275); an average **50-mile** round trip for biometrics (**91 FR 45083**); PRA time-burden estimates of **1 hour** (Form I-539 e-file), **1.667 hours** (Form I-539 paper), **0.35 hours** (Supplement A / I-539A), and **1.17 hours** (biometrics), with **$83,736,379** total annual PRA cost burden across all I-539 respondents (**91 FR 45120**); and **$317.9 million** (3% discount) / **$317.3 million** (7% discount) in annualized EOS costs to nonimmigrants (**91 FR 45116**). **(iii) Commenter statements only (NOT DHS authority):** All specific per-filing fee figures in the rule appear solely in summaries of public comments—one commenter cited a **$420** filing fee (**91 FR 45055**) and another cited **~$1,680** for four EOS filings (**91 FR 45082**, i.e., $420 × 4), while others cited **$555** including biometrics (**91 FR 45065**), **$367 to over $800** (**91 FR 45056**), and **$750 to $3,000** for private legal counsel (**91 FR 45082**). **(2) How Long USCIS Takes to Decide Form I-539:** **(i) DHS preamble text:** DHS explicitly states that **DHS 'cannot guarantee processing times'**, that processing times are **'subject to change'**, and that the rule **'may cause an increase in USCIS processing times'** (**91 FR 45009, 45021, 45025, 45029, 45031, 45083–45084**), directing readers to USCIS's online Case Processing Times page (`https://egov.uscis.gov/processing-times/`, **91 FR 45084** fn. 277) and noting premium processing is not currently available for these EOS filings though DHS will continue to explore expanding it (**91 FR 45051–45052**). DHS states *EAD* (Form I-765) processing times are *'typically **60–120 days** for foreign students and **90–120 [days]** for most others'* (**91 FR 45032, 45107**), encourages filing EOS within **6 months (180 days)** before stay expires (**91 FR 45043, 45106–45107, 45110**), and provides up to **240 days** of automatic employment continuation while a timely EOS is pending (**8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)**). **(ii) Commenter statements only (NOT DHS authority):** Every specific Form I-539 processing-time number in the rule comes from commenters, who reported **~3.5 months** for extensions (and **4.5 months** for changes to F-1/J-1 at the California Service Center, **91 FR 44999, 45083**), **more than 6.5 months** for Service Center Operations to decide 80% of EOS requests (**91 FR 45063**), and ranges **often exceeding 240 days**, **6 to 19 months**, **12 to 18 months**, or **up to 18 months** during backlogs (**91 FR 45031, 45036, 45048, 45051**). **(3) Accurate Draft Handout Text (2 sentences):** *'To extend your F-1 stay in the United States, you must file Form I-539 with USCIS and pay the current Form I-539 filing fee listed on USCIS's fee schedule (one filing fee covers both you and any F-2 dependents included on Form I-539A, and biometrics may also be required). USCIS does not guarantee Form I-539 processing times—which vary and should be checked at egov.uscis.gov/processing-times—so DHS recommends applying up to 6 months (180 days) before your current stay expires to avoid interruptions in work authorization.'*
Q11.uncertainty: Because the final rule text refers to the separately docketed Regulatory Impact Analysis (Table 16) rather than printing the current Form I-539 dollar fee in the Federal Register—and provides no agency-verified Form I-539 processing-time baseline—an adviser relying solely on the final rule cannot state a guaranteed dollar fee or adjudication timeframe without pointing students to current USCIS form instructions and processing-time postings.

Q12.answer: **(a) Is an I-539 Received During Priya's 60-Day Departure Period Timely?** **Yes** (provided that, if she is extending her *current* bachelor's program rather than transferring/changing degree levels, her DSO entered the program extension in SEVIS on or before her May 15, 2027 program end date as required by **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(viii)**). Under final regulatory text at **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)** (added by **2026-14439**), as a D/S transition student maintaining status on September 15, 2026, Priya is authorized to remain in F-1 status until her I-20 program end date (**May 15, 2027**) **plus a 60-day departure period** (through **July 14, 2027**). Under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)**, an EOS application is timely filed if USCIS's receipt date (`8 CFR 103.2(a)(7)`) is **on or before the date the authorized period of stay expires**, and preamble Section V.E.1 (**91 FR 45101**) explicitly confirms that D/S transition F-1 students may file an EOS request up to their program end date **plus the additional 60 days**. **(b) Does She Keep the Automatic Extension of On-Campus or CPT Employment If She Files During Those 60 Days?** **No.** If USCIS receives her Form I-539 after May 15, 2027 (during the 60-day departure period of May 16 – July 14, 2027), she may remain in the U.S. and continue studying, **but she receives NO automatic extension of on-campus or CPT employment** and must wait until USCIS approves the Form I-539 before engaging in employment or CPT. Three provisions establish this: **(1) 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)** explicitly provides that for D/S transition students, *'any authorized employment or training continues **until the program end date** on such F or J nonimmigrant's Form I-20'* (May 15, 2027)—meaning her underlying on-campus and CPT work authorization ends on May 15, 2027 and does not continue into the 60-day departure period; **(2) 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)** and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)** bar any automatic extension of on-campus, CPT, or hardship employment when an EOS is filed during the post-program departure period (and note that CPT also cannot extend past the DSO-authorized CPT end date on Form I-20); and **(3)** for Form I-9 verification under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)**, Priya lacks an unexpired employment period (and lacks a fixed-date Form I-94) once May 15, 2027 passes. **Recommendation for the Adviser:** Advise Priya that **(1)** if she wants uninterrupted on-campus or CPT work authorization, her DSO must update SEVIS and **USCIS must receive her Form I-539 on or before May 15, 2027** (ideally up to 6 months early per DHS's recommendation at **91 FR 45106–45107, 45110**, so she also has her Form I-797C receipt notice in hand by May 15, 2027 for Form I-9 purposes); **(2)** if she is extending her *current* program, the DSO **must** enter the SEVIS extension on or before **May 15, 2027** regardless of when she files with USCIS, or else she falls out of status and needs reinstatement (**8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(viii)**); and **(3)** if she does not need summer work authorization (e.g., transferring to a fall master's program), while filing through **July 14, 2027** is timely under `214.1(m)(1)`, having USCIS receive the I-539 within the first 30 days (**on or before June 14, 2027**) is the safest practice to avoid any literal cross-reference friction with `214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)`'s reference to 'the 30-day period.'
Q12.uncertainty: **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)** and **214.2(f)(5)(viii)** were drafted around the permanent regime and therefore refer to *'the 30-day period provided in paragraph (f)(5)(v)'* rather than cross-referencing **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)**'s 60-day transition departure period. For **part (a)**, `8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)` (defining authorized stay through 60 days; see also `(m)(1)(i)` *'before his or her period of admission expires, including the 60 day departure period'*) and preamble **91 FR 45101** make clear the full 60 days is timely, though filing within 30 days avoids any literalist objection. Conversely, for **part (b)**, a student could not plausibly claim an employment extension by arguing the 60-day `(m)(1)` period is not the `(f)(5)(v)` 30-day period, because `214.1(m)(1)` expressly terminates employment at the May 15, 2027 program end date.

Q13.answer: **(a) Authorized Stay After January 9, 2027 Readmission Without Filing Anything:** **June 13, 2027.** Because Sofia departed the United States after September 15, 2026 and sought readmission on January 9, 2027, she exited the `8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)` D/S transition regime (losing its 60-day departure period) and was admitted with a **fixed period of admission** under **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)**, **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)**, and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)** (confirmed by **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii)** and preamble **91 FR 45018, 45099, 45101**). Her fixed admission runs to her Form I-20 program end date (**May 14, 2027**, < 4 years) **plus a 30-day departure period**. *Date arithmetic:* **May 14, 2027** + **30 days**: $31 - 14 = 17$ remaining days in May (to May 31, 2027) + $13$ days in June ($30 - 17 = 13$) = **June 13, 2027**. **(b) Form I-539 Requirement and Filing Deadline:** **Yes, she MUST file Form I-539**, even though she files Form I-765 on February 22, 2027 (before the March 18, 2027 transition exemption cutoff). Final regulatory text at **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii)** explicitly provides that a D/S transition student *'who departs the United States **before filing** the application for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT, and is admitted to the United States with a fixed period of admission **is required to file both** an Application for Employment Authorization, Form I-765 ... **and** an Application to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status, Form I-539'* (see also **8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D)**). *(Note: her requested June 10, 2027 OPT start date is 27 days after May 14, 2027, satisfying **8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(D)**'s 30-day limit.)* **Deadline:** Under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)** (and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2)** as amended at **91 FR 45124**), USCIS must receive her Form I-539 **on or before June 13, 2027** (the expiration of her authorized stay including the 30-day departure period; DHS recommends concurrent filing with Form I-765 on February 22, 2027, **91 FR 45033**, and `214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2)` also requires OPT filings within 30 days of the DSO's SEVIS recommendation). **(c) Authorized Stay If Approved as Requested (OPT Through June 9, 2028):** **July 9, 2028.** Under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D)**, **214.2(f)(7)(vi)**, and **214.2(f)(5)(v)**, an approved EOS for post-completion OPT includes an **additional 30-day departure period** after the approved OPT end date. *Date arithmetic:* **June 9, 2028** + **30 days**: $30 - 9 = 21$ remaining days in June (to June 30, 2028) + $9$ days in July ($30 - 21 = 9$) = **July 9, 2028**. **(d) Alternative Facts (No December Travel; Files I-765 Feb. 22, 2027; Travels May 20 – June 5, 2027 While I-765 Is Pending):** **(1) Form I-539 needed?** **No.** Because she was still in D/S transition status when she filed Form I-765 on February 22, 2027 (on or before March 18, 2027), **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i)** exempted her from filing Form I-539; and when she later departs on May 20, 2027 *while Form I-765 is pending*, the second sentence of **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii)** provides that she will be admitted at the port of entry pursuant to **8 CFR 214.1(a)** (specifically **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii)**; see also **8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D)**, permitting OPT stay via CBP admission after travel abroad, and **8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii)**, confirming travel does not abandon a pending I-765). **(2) Period of readmission on June 5, 2027:** Under **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii)**, because her Form I-765 is pending, CBP may admit her **until the DSO's recommended OPT employment end date on Form I-20 (June 9, 2028) plus a 30-day departure period** under `8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)` = **July 9, 2028** (note that traveling converts her from `(m)(1)(i)`'s 60-day post-EAD departure period to `(a)(4)(iii)`'s 30-day departure period). **(3) What she should carry:** Under **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(iii)** and **8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(iii)** (and preamble **91 FR 45098, 45100** fn. 303), she should carry: **(i)** her **USCIS receipt notice (Form I-797C)** for the pending **Form I-765**; **(ii)** her **latest signed Form I-20 endorsed by her DSO** recommending post-completion OPT with the proposed end date (June 9, 2028); and **(iii)** a **valid passport** and **valid F-1 visa** (if required), while ensuring someone monitors her U.S. mail for any RFE or delivered EAD.
Q13.uncertainty: In part (b), **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii)** cross-references `8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2)`, which requires post-completion OPT filings to be submitted within 30 days after the DSO enters the OPT recommendation in SEVIS (and no later than 30 days after the program end date). While **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)** allows Form I-539 to be received anytime through June 13, 2027, whether USCIS treats `214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2)`'s 30-day-from-DSO-endorsement rule as applying solely to Form I-765 or also to an OPT-based Form I-539 is not explicitly spelled out; filing Form I-539 concurrently with Form I-765 on February 22, 2027 satisfies both rules. In part (d), preamble **91 FR 45100** fn. 303 warns that if USCIS approves Form I-765 *while* Sofia is abroad (May 20 – June 5, 2027), she would be expected to have the physical EAD in hand at re-entry.

Q14.answer: **(a) Document Identification, Metadata, Status, and Deadlines:** FR Document Number **2026-20660**, titled *Optional Practical Training Fees*, citation **91 FR 64566** (pages **64566–64600**, published **October 8, 2026**); **type:** **Proposed Rule** (Notice of Proposed Rulemaking / NPRM); **agency:** **U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Department of Homeland Security (DHS)**; **docket:** **DHS Docket No. ICEB-2026-0100**; **RIN:** **1653-AB01**. **Current status and deadlines:** **Proposed rule, not finalized and not in force** as of November 14, 2026. It sets three timelines/deadlines: **(1) NPRM public comment deadline:** **November 9, 2026** (closed; **91 FR 64566**); **(2) Paperwork Reduction Act (information collection) comment deadline:** **December 7, 2026** (still open; **91 FR 64566**); and **(3) Proposed effective date / transition trigger:** **60 days after the date of publication of the final rule** in the Federal Register (`proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3)`, **91 FR 64577, 64600**). **(b) Amount Applicable to Daniel's STEM OPT Extension Under the Proposed Text:** **$70,000 (NOT $30,000).** Under `proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)` (**91 FR 64600**), the lower **$30,000** subsequent OPT fee applies **only** *'if the alien has previously participated in OPT **and paid the initial OPT fee of $70,000**'*, and the transition provision at `proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3)` (**91 FR 64600**; echoed verbatim in preamble Section V.C, **91 FR 64577**) explicitly states that schools *'recommending **any type of OPT** for an alien **must pay the fee of $70,000** for each alien who receives a DSO recommendation for OPT that is dated on or after [60 DAYS AFTER DATE OF PUBLICATION OF THE FINAL RULE]. Thereafter, any subsequent DSO recommendations for OPT issued for any F-1 student who has previously participated in OPT, **and for which the $70,000 OPT fee has been paid**, will be subject to the subsequent OPT fee of $30,000 per alien.'* Because Daniel obtained his current post-completion OPT in 2026 *before* any $70,000 OPT fee existed or was paid, his April 2027 STEM OPT recommendation would require the **$70,000** payment under `proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)–(3)`. **(c) Who Pays, When, Consequences of Non-Payment, and Refundability:** **(1) Who pays:** The **SEVP-certified educational institution (school)** (`proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(ii), 214.13(i)(1)–(3)`, **91 FR 64599–64600**; deposited into the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, **91 FR 64576**). **(2) When:** **Prior to the DSO issuing/entering the OPT recommendation in SEVIS** (and before the student files Form I-765; the DSO must verify payment, enter payment details in SEVIS, and issue a signed Form I-20 confirming payment, `proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i), (ii)(B)–(C)`). **(3) Consequences of non-payment:** The DSO **may not enter the OPT recommendation in SEVIS** (**91 FR 64577**), and **USCIS may not grant employment authorization** where the DSO issued the recommendation before the school paid the fee or where the school failed to pay all required OPT fees (`proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(iii)`, **91 FR 64599**). **(4) Refundability:** **Discretionary/conditional before EAD issuance, and strictly nonrefundable after approval:** SEVP may, in its unappealable case-by-case discretion, grant a school's refund request **only if** the student **has not been issued/granted the EAD or OPT extension** AND the DSO **first removes the OPT recommendation in SEVIS**; once the EAD/extension is granted or issued, **the fee will not be refunded under any circumstances** (`proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2)`, **91 FR 64577, 64600**). **(d) Trigger Date and Whether DSO Recommendation Timing Could Keep Daniel Outside It:** Under `proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(3)`, the fee applies to **DSO recommendations dated on or after the final rule's effective date** (60 days after final rule publication). **Yes, DSO timing could keep Daniel outside it** if the DSO validly dates and enters the STEM OPT recommendation **before the final rule's effective date** (rather than waiting until after it takes effect in April 2027): under existing STEM OPT rules (`8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(C)`), USCIS accepts STEM OPT Form I-765 filings up to **90 days before** the current EAD expires (June 30, 2027 minus 90 days = **April 1, 2027**: $30$ days in June + $31$ in May + $29$ in April = April 1, 2027) and requires Form I-765 to be filed within **60 days** after the DSO enters the STEM OPT recommendation in SEVIS—so if the rule took effect on, say, April 5, 2027, recommending on April 1–4, 2027 (or earlier in February/March 2027 if SEVIS permits DSO entry within 60 days prior to an April 1+ filing) would predate the effective date and avoid the fee. **(e) Under Rules in Force Today (Nov. 14, 2026) for an April 12, 2027 Filing:** **(1) What Daniel must file:** Because April 12, 2027 is **after March 18, 2027** (the cutoff for the D/S transition I-539 exemption in **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i)**, added by **2026-14439**; note his 90-day STEM OPT window only opens April 1, 2027), under **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)** and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(v)** he must file **both Form I-765** (for the 24-month STEM OPT EAD) **and Form I-539** (EOS, with fee, endorsed Form I-20, proof of funds, and biometrics if required) on or before June 30, 2027. **(2) Work authorization while pending:** Under **8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv)** (expressly confirmed by **2026-14439** preamble **91 FR 45101** and unaffected by **2026-20955**, **91 FR 65307**), his OPT EAD is **automatically extended for up to 180 days** past June 30, 2027 (through **December 27, 2027**: $31$ Jul. + $31$ Aug. + $30$ Sep. + $31$ Oct. + $30$ Nov. = 153 + $27$ Dec. = 180 days, or until USCIS adjudicates, whichever is earlier), while his timely EOS keeps him in authorized stay (**8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)**). **(3) Authorized stay if approved:** A 24-month STEM OPT extension runs **July 1, 2027 through June 30, 2029**, plus the **30-day departure period** under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi)** and **214.2(f)(5)(v)** (preamble **91 FR 45105**) = **July 30, 2029** (June 30, 2029 + 30 days).
Q14.uncertainty: In **part (b)**, there is a slight drafting tension in **2026-20660** between `proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)` (which refers to *'the first time that the alien is recommended to participate in OPT'*) and `proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)–(3)` (which explicitly govern transition cases, require $70,000 for *'any type of OPT'* recommended on or after the effective date, and limit the $30,000 fee to students *'for which the $70,000 OPT fee has been paid'*); the specific transition rule in `(i)(3)` controls the proposed text, though commenters may press DHS to clarify or revise this if finalized (and DHS also solicited comment on an alternative charging $70,000 at each new degree level, **91 FR 64577**). The proposed rule is also silent on whether schools may pass the fee on to students or employers. In **part (d)**, `8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(C)` was not printed in the FR amendments, so whether SEVIS technically allows a DSO to enter a STEM OPT recommendation more than 90 days before EAD expiration (for filing inside the 90-day window) cannot be verified from the FR alone. In **part (e)**, if DHS later published a 6-month extension of the March 18, 2027 exemption under **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(iii)** before April 12, 2027, Daniel would not need Form I-539 and would get 60 days (to August 29, 2029) upon approval.

Q15.answer: **(1) Statement 1 — Incorrect:** Under final regulatory text at **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)** and **214.2(f)(5)(v)** (**91 FR 45125–45126**), USCIS may timely receive an EOS application **on or before the date the student's authorized period of stay expires, which includes the 30-day departure period** after the program end date (or 60-day departure period for D/S transition students under **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)**)—though filing during that departure period forfeits automatic extension of employment (**8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii), (f)(7)(iii)(B)**), and if extending a *current* program end date, the **DSO** must enter the extension in SEVIS on or before the current I-20 program end date (**8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(viii)**). *(Note: preamble **91 FR 45039** loosely says 'prior to the expiration,' whereas regulatory text **214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)** says **'on or before'**; regulatory text controls.)* *Rewording:* *'To be timely, USCIS must receive an extension-of-stay application on or before your authorized stay expires (including your post-program departure period), though to keep working without interruption—and for your DSO to extend a current I-20—action must be taken on or before your I-20 program end date.'* **(2) Statement 2 — Incorrect:** Final regulatory text at **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)** (**91 FR 45124**) provides that the 30-day arrival period before the I-20 report/program start date (and 30-day departure period) **do not count toward the 4-year maximum**, and preamble Section V.B (**91 FR 45098**) confirms that when a student enters during the 30-day pre-arrival window, the 4-year maximum runs **from the program start date, not the entry date** (though on a mid-program readmission after the start date has passed, CBP measures up to 4 years from readmission). *Rewording:* *'For students entering up to 30 days before their program begins, the four-year maximum admission period is counted from the Form I-20 program start date (or report date), not the date of entry, plus a 30-day departure period.'* **(3) Statement 3 — Correct (with one precondition):** Assuming the EOS was timely filed *before* the 30-day departure period began (and the academic program itself has not ended), **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)** (**91 FR 45125–45126**) and preamble **91 FR 45043, 45106** authorize the student to remain in an authorized stay and keep pursuing a full course of study until USCIS decides the EOS, while capping the automatic extension of on-campus employment at **240 days from the Form I-94 expiration date**. *Rewording (for precision):* *'If a student files an extension of stay on or before their program end date and USCIS has still not decided it 240 days after the Form I-94 expiration date, the student may stay and keep studying full-time while it remains pending, but must stop any on-campus job until USCIS approves the extension.'* **(4) Statement 4 — Incorrect:** **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A)** (**91 FR 45124**) restricts standalone English language training (ELT) students to a **maximum admission period of 24 months** (plus 30 days for departure), and preamble Section IV.J.1.b (**91 FR 45039**, lines 8131–8134; see also **91 FR 45103, 45110**) explicitly states: *'Students who encounter extenuating circumstances such as illness, disability, or other emergencies during their studies, **will still be limited to the 24-month admission period**.'* *Rewording:* *'Students in standalone English language training programs are capped at an aggregate 24 months of study (plus 30 days to depart) and cannot extend an ELT stay beyond 24 months even for serious illness (except D/S transition students finishing an existing I-20 up to 4 years or students in an integrated degree-pathway program).' * **(5) Statement 5 — Incorrect:** Under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)** and **214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(1)** (**91 FR 45124, 45126**), the 4-year limit caps the *admission period granted by DHS*, not the length of an accredited program on Form I-20; preamble Section IV.J.1.b (**91 FR 45039–45040**) expressly rejects this misconception, explaining that a 5-year accredited program's Form I-20 **will state the full 5-year program length** and the student simply applies for an EOS using **that same Form I-20**. *Rewording:* *'A degree program accredited as a five-year program is still issued on a single Form I-20 showing the full five-year length; the student is initially admitted for four years (plus 30 days) and files an extension of stay with USCIS using that same I-20 to finish the fifth year.'* **(6) Statement 6 — Partly correct:** Under **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)–(B)** and **214.2(f)(5)(i)** (**91 FR 45122, 45124**; preamble **91 FR 45098, 45100**), CBP *may* admit a returning student with a valid F-1 visa on an updated Form I-20 for up to the later program end date (**capped at 4 years**, plus 30 days), obviating a USCIS EOS for *that* admitted period; **however**, CBP admission is discretionary, is **capped at 4 years**, does **not** extend stay beyond the prior unexpired period if re-entering with an expired visa under contiguous-territory/adjacent-island automatic visa revalidation (**8 CFR 214.1(b)(1)**, **91 FR 45122**), cannot cure a late DSO extension (**214.2(f)(7)(viii)**) or prohibited level/program change (**214.2(f)(5)(ii)**), and does not replace **Form I-765** for OPT (**214.1(c)(8)(ii), 214.2(f)(10)(ii)(D)**). *Rewording:* *'A maintaining-status student with a valid F-1 visa who travels and is readmitted on a valid I-20 with a later program end date may be granted a new CBP admission period of up to four years (plus 30 days)—avoiding a USCIS extension for that period—unless re-entering under automatic visa revalidation with an expired visa, which only restores the prior unexpired stay.'* **(7) Statement 7 — Incorrect (Regulatory Text vs. Preamble Divergence):** Several **preamble** passages describe the OPT/STEM OPT Form I-539 exemption loosely as covering filings *'during the first 6 months after the rule takes effect'* (**91 FR 44978**) or *'within six months of the effective date'* (**91 FR 45033, 45034**)—and one preamble sentence (**91 FR 45101**, lines 15696–15697) even mistakenly says *'on or before September 15, 2026'*—**whereas final regulatory text at 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(i) (91 FR 45123)** sets the binding deadline as **'on or before March 18, 2027'** (and limits eligibility to **D/S transition students** who have **not** departed and been readmitted with a fixed date prior to filing Form I-765, **8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)(ii)**). **The final regulatory text controls**, so the last filing day is **March 18, 2027**, not March 15, 2027. *Rewording:* *'F-1 students in the D/S transition group who have not traveled and re-entered on a fixed admission date do not need to file Form I-539 for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT if USCIS timely receives their Form I-765 on or before March 18, 2027 (unless DHS extends this date by Federal Register notice).' *
Q15.uncertainty: For Statement 3, as noted in **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)** (**91 FR 45125–45126**), Sentence 2 measures the 240-day cap from the Form I-94 expiration date while Sentence 5 (on Form I-9 verification) refers to the employment period ending 30 days before the Form I-94 admit-until date; Sentence 2 and preamble **91 FR 45106** directly support measuring the 240-day cap from the I-94 date. For Statement 6, if a student with *no* pending or approved EOS travels *before* their existing I-94 expires, **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)** has a minor drafting gap (discussed in detail where relevant, as `(A)` mentions expired prior stays), making verification of the new CBP I-94 essential.

Q16.answer: **(a) Lin's Form I-94 Admit-Until Date:** **September 22, 2031.** Under final regulatory text at **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)**, **214.2(f)(5)(v)**, and **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)** (**91 FR 45122, 45124–45125**), an F-1 student in a program exceeding 4 years is admitted for a **4-year maximum period** plus a **30-day departure period**, and the 30-day pre-program arrival window (here August 2 to August 23, 2027) **does not count** toward the 4-year maximum—as preamble Section V.B (**91 FR 45098**) confirms, the 4-year period is calculated **from the program start date** (**August 23, 2027**). *Date arithmetic (using DHS's anniversary-date method reflected in `8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)`, where Sept. 15, 2026 + 4 years = Sept. 15, 2030):* **August 23, 2027** + **4 years** = **August 23, 2031**; adding **30 days**: $31 - 23 = 8$ remaining days in August 2031 (to Aug. 31, 2031) + $22$ days in September ($30 - 8 = 22$) = **September 22, 2031**. **(b) Extending Stay Beyond September 22, 2031:** **(1) Action & submission:** Unless she obtains a new admission period from CBP via travel abroad, Lin must timely file an **extension of stay (EOS) on Form I-539** with USCIS on or before September 22, 2031 (**8 CFR 214.1(c)(2)**, **214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A)–(B)**), submitting: **(i)** Form I-539; **(ii)** her currently issued, valid, DSO-endorsed **Form I-20** showing her May 14, 2033 program end date (preamble **91 FR 45039** confirms a multi-year student uses the same full-length I-20); **(iii)** **evidence of sufficient funds** to cover expenses (readily available funds for one year plus reliable sources for the remainder, **91 FR 45110**); **(iv)** the **required filing fee**; and **(v)** any **biometrics** required under `8 CFR 103.16`. **(2) Ground for grant:** **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(1)**—having continually maintained status `(A)` and pursuing a full course of study `(B)` with *'A currently issued Form I-20, or successor form, indicating additional time is left to complete his or her program of study'* (preamble **91 FR 45108–45109** also notes standard >4-year doctoral timelines constitute compelling academic reasons). **(3) How early she may file:** Preamble footnotes 197, 328, and 338 (**91 FR 45040, 45107, 45110**) state **there is no regulatory prohibition on filing Form I-539 before a specific date ahead of expiration**, while DHS **recommends filing within 6 months (180 days) before expiration** (**91 FR 45043, 45106–45107, 45110**—i.e., from around **March 22–26, 2031**; and if she has an on-campus job/assistantship, she must file on or before **August 23, 2031** to preserve the 240-day employment auto-extension under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii)**). **(4) New stay end date if granted in full:** Because remaining program time to **May 14, 2033** is under 4 years, **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(vi)** and **(f)(5)(v)** (**91 FR 45105, 45125–45126**) grant through **May 14, 2033** + **30 days** ($31 - 14 = 17$ days in May + $13$ days in June) = **June 13, 2033**. **(c) Effect of Receiving an En-Route Master's Degree in 2029:** **None—it does not affect her ability to finish the PhD in F-1 status.** Her primary educational objective on Form I-20 has not changed (**8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A)**), a PhD is higher—not the same or lower—than a master's (**8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(B)–(C)**), and preamble Section IV.J.1.f (**91 FR 45042–45043**) explicitly confirms that *'a student issued a Form I-20 for a Ph.D. program as their primary academic objective could obtain a master's degree incidental to status while progressing toward completion of the Ph.D. program.'* **(d) August 2030 Three-Week Trip Abroad (No EOS Pending) and Certainty:** **Most defensible reading:** Under **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)** and preamble **91 FR 45040** (*'If the student travels abroad, the stay will be extended for a four-year maximum every time the ... student travels abroad'*) and **91 FR 45098**, if Lin re-enters with a valid F-1 visa on her valid Form I-20 (whose May 14, 2033 end date is now < 4 years away), CBP **may admit her through May 14, 2033 + 30 days = June 13, 2033**, in which case **she would NO LONGER need the Form I-539 filing in (b)**. **Level of certainty — Moderate / Contingent (NOT 100% certain), for three reasons:** **(1) Drafting gap in 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i):** Subparagraph `(A)` expressly addresses readmission *'after a previously authorized period of admission ... expired'*, `(B)` covers pending EOS, and `(C)` covers approved EOS—leaving unstated in `214.1(a)(4)(i)` itself whether a student returning *before* her initial stay expires (with no pending/approved EOS) receives a fresh up-to-4-year admission or only her unexpired prior balance (Sept. 22, 2031); **(2) CBP discretion:** Even under the preamble, CBP *'may'* admit up to 4 years (**91 FR 45098–45099**); and **(3) Missing travel/visa facts:** Because her 21-day trip is ≤ 30 days, if her F-1 visa has expired and she re-enters from Canada/Mexico/adjacent islands under **automatic visa revalidation** (**8 CFR 214.1(b)(1)**, **91 FR 45122**), CBP may admit her **only up to her unexpired prior stay (September 22, 2031)**, so she **would still need** the EOS in (b). Lin must inspect her August 2030 Form I-94 upon return. **(e) F-2 Husband's Later 2031 I-94 Date, Coverage on Lin's EOS, and Fee:** **(1) Until when he may stay:** Only **until the expiration of Lin's authorized F-1 period of stay** (not the later date erroneously printed on his I-94, unless Lin's own stay is extended), because final regulatory text at **8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(i)(E)** and **214.2(f)(7)(vi)** (**91 FR 45124, 45126**) mandates that *'The authorized period of stay for F-2 dependents **may not exceed** the authorized period of stay of the principal F-1 student.'* **(2) How he is covered when Lin applies under (b):** Under **8 CFR 214.1(c)(2)** and **8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iv)** (**91 FR 45123, 45126**), he may either be **included as a co-applicant on Lin's Form I-539** (by submitting **Form I-539A**, preamble **91 FR 45110**) or **file his own separate Form I-539** (demonstrating qualifying relationship, status maintenance, no unauthorized work, updated I-20, financial support, and any required biometrics). **(3) Fee:** Preamble Section V.F.5 (**91 FR 45110**; see also **91 FR 45013**) states that if he files **Form I-539A** as part of Lin's Form I-539, **only one Form I-539 filing fee is required**; if he files a **separate Form I-539**, he must pay a **separate Form I-539 filing fee**.
Q16.uncertainty: In **part (a)**, while DHS's anniversary-date convention in `8 CFR 214.1(m)(1)` yields August 23, 2031 + 30 days = September 22, 2031, inclusive-day counting by CBP (Aug. 23, 2027 through Aug. 22, 2031 + 30 days = September 21, 2031) or an erroneous calculation from entry date (Sept. 1, 2031) could shift the I-94 by 1 or 21 days, so checking the actual Form I-94 is prudent. In **part (d)**, as explained above, the omission in **8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(A)–(C)** of returning students with unexpired stay and no pending/approved EOS, combined with CBP discretion and unknown visa/destination facts for her 21-day August 2030 trip, leaves open whether CBP will grant June 13, 2033 or September 22, 2031.
